Great contrast means brilliant white patterns on a deep, rich brown background.

Poor contrast means grey, washed-out, or muddy patterns.

### How to Improve Contrast

| Factor | Action |
|---|---|
| Fresher espresso | Always pour immediately after extraction |
| Better crema | Improve extraction — dial in correctly |
| Proper milk texture | Glossy, silky, fully integrated |
| Jug position | Get closer to the surface |
| Better integration | High pour phase properly sinks the foam |
| Service speed | Don't let espresso sit — crema degrades in seconds |

The single biggest contrast killer: Old espresso. Crema begins to degrade the moment extraction ends. After 30–45 seconds, the contrast drops dramatically. Pour immediately.

---

## Symmetry

Symmetry is the most common criterion in competition judging.

Judges look for:
- Balance — left and right sides of the pattern are equal
- Equal wings — rosetta leaves and tulip layers match each side
- Even spacing — layers are equidistant from each other
- Centre alignment — the pattern sits in the centre of the cup

### How to Train Symmetry

- Straight cut-throughs: Practise cutting through the exact centre every time
- Consistent cup angle: Keep the tilt angle constant through the pour
- Stable wrist position: If the wrist drifts, the centre drifts
- Controlled flow: Inconsistent flow = uneven layers

Exercise: Pour 20 hearts, photograph each one, compare the symmetry. The visual record reveals patterns your hands can't feel during the pour.

---

## Flow Control Mastery

The best Australian baristas master five distinct flow states:

| State | Description | Used For |
|---|---|---|
| Thick flow | Wide, fast stream | Rosetta base, tulip body |
| Medium flow | Standard café pace | Most pours |
| Thin flow | Fine, slow stream | Swan neck, rosetta details |
| Stop-start | Deliberate flow pause | Between tulip pushes |
| Taper | Gradually slowing | Finishing and cut-through transitions |

### Flow Drills

Use water only — no espresso waste:

- Draw 10 circles of the same size
- Draw 10 straight lines of equal width
- Practise rapid flow changes: fast → stop → slow → stop
- Practise thin-stream pours (swan necks) across the surface of the water
- Time yourself: pour 10 clean cut-through lines in under 5 minutes
key_points: Contrast is destroyed by old espresso — pour immediately after extraction
Symmetry: equal balance, centred pattern, consistent cut-throughs
Film your pours to see symmetry issues your hands can't feel
Master 5 flow states: thick, medium, thin, stop-start, and taper

lessons.title: Common Latte Art Failures
lessons.content:
## Common Latte Art Failures

Every barista hits these problems. Understanding the cause behind each failure turns frustrating repetition into systematic improvement.

---

## Big Bubbles on the Surface

Cause: Poor milk texturing — tip too far from surface during stretch phase, or insufficient rolling

Fix: More thorough whirlpool rolling phase. Ensure the stretch was brief and the tip was at the surface, not above it.

---

## Washed-Out Art / No White Visible

Cause: Jug still too high when pattern should be forming. Foam sinks instead of rising.

Fix: Commit to getting the jug down. The jug should be almost touching the crema surface when art is forming.

---

## White Blobs Instead of Patterns

Cause: Milk too thick — too much air stretched in, or over-textured

Fix: Less aeration. Stretch phase should be very brief for latte art. More stretching = thicker foam = less pourable = blobs.

---

## No Contrast / Grey Pattern

Cause: Dead or old crema. Espresso sat too long before pouring.

Fix: Fresh extraction. Pour immediately. Never let espresso sit more than 30 seconds before adding milk.

---

## Splitting

Cause: Milk separated in the jug — foam has risen to the top and water sank to the bottom.

Fix: Swirl the jug immediately before pouring. If the milk has separated (visible watery layer at bottom), discard and start again.

---

## Jagged, Uneven Lines

Cause: Unstable wrist. Tension in the pouring hand.

Fix: Consciously relax the grip and wrist. The wrist should feel loose, not gripped. Most baristas discover they're holding the jug far too tightly.

---

## Pattern Sits on One Side

Cause: Jug angled toward one side of the cup, or cup not level

Fix: Check cup angle. Aim the pour at the exact centre of the cup. The tip of the jug spout should point to the centre at all times.

---

## Rosetta Won't Separate Into Leaves

Cause: Not moving backward, OR wiggle rate too slow

Fix: Start backward movement immediately as the jug lowers. Don't wait. Also check wiggle rhythm is consistent.

---

## Quick Diagnosis Table

| What You See | Root Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Blobs | Over-stretched milk | Less air during stretch |
| Washed-out pattern | Jug too high | Get closer |
| No contrast | Old espresso | Pour immediately |
| Bubbles | Poor rolling phase | More whirlpool |
| Splitting | Milk separated | Swirl before pouring |
| Jagged lines | Tense wrist | Relax grip |
| Off-centre pattern | Jug aimed sideways | Aim at exact centre |
key_points: Blobs = over-stretched milk; get less air in
Washed-out art = jug too high; commit to getting down close
No contrast = old espresso; pour immediately after extraction
Jagged lines = tense wrist; consciously relax the grip

quiz.question: Your latte art looks washed out and grey — the pattern is barely visible. You have good milk texture. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The milk temperature is too low — steam hotter
The espresso is over-extracted — dial coarser
The jug is too high when the pattern should form — get the jug closer to the surface
The cup is too large for the amount of milk
quiz.explanation: Washed-out, grey art with poor contrast is almost always caused by the jug being too high. When the jug is far from the surface, foam sinks beneath the crema instead of rising through it. Getting the jug close to the crema surface is the fix.

lessons.title: Competition Techniques & Advanced Pours
lessons.content:
## Competition Techniques & Advanced Pours

Competition latte art is an extension of café latte art — not a different skill. The same fundamentals apply, but with more precision, slower movement, and better preparation.

---

## What Competition Judges Evaluate

- Layer density — depth and volume of foam structure
- Fine detail — thin lines, small elements, precision shapes
- Symmetry — are both halves of the pattern equal?
- Contrast — how white is the white? How dark is the dark?
- Complexity — how many elements are in the design?
- Overall impression — does it look effortless?

---

## Popular Australian Competition Pours

| Pour | Description |
|---|---|
| Winged tulip | Tulip stacks with side flow additions — wide, bold |
| Triple swan | Three swans in the one cup — requires extraordinary control |
| Pegasus swan | Swan variant with additional wing detail |
| Rosetta-tulip | Rosetta leaves emerging from a tulip body |
| Ripple tulip | Tulip stacks with ripple texture on each layer |
| Fine-line swan | Swan with an extremely thin neck — technical precision required |

---

## Winged Tulip

Adds side wings to each tulip stack.

Technique:
- Standard tulip push
- After each push, briefly widen the pour to create side extensions
- Requires wider flow and slight sideways jug movement per layer

Very common in both Melbourne and Sydney competition routines.

---

## Competition Pour Strategy

Great competition pours require:
- Slower movement — speed destroys precision
- Better milk — slightly cooler (55–60°C) for more working time
- Lower jug height — maximum contrast at all times
- More refined flow — the flow must be fully controlled, not just guided
- Perfect crema — no compromise on espresso quality

---

## Building Competition Skills

1. Master basic patterns until they are automatic — there should be no conscious thought when executing a heart, tulip, or rosetta
2. Add one new element at a time — never attempt a full swan if you haven't mastered the thin neck pour alone
3. Film every pour — video reveals symmetry problems and wrist movement issues invisible in real time
4. Enter competitions early — performing under pressure is a separate skill that only develops under pressure
5. Study footage — watch Australian Latte Art Championship and World Latte Art Championship videos

---

## The Most Important Competition Truth

> The simpler the design appears, the more skill it usually required.

A perfect, symmetrical, high-contrast 3-stack tulip beats a messy swan every time. Build mastery in the fundamentals before complexity.
key_points: Competition judging: contrast, symmetry, density, fine detail, complexity
Winged tulip is one of Australia's most common competition pours
Film every pour — video reveals what hands can't feel
Enter competitions early — pressure under judging is a separate skill

lessons.title: Australian Café Styles & Assessment
lessons.content:
## Australian Café Styles & Practical Assessment

---

## Australian Regional Café Styles

Latte art style varies by city — shaped by local competition culture, café aesthetics, and customer expectations.

### Melbourne Style

Characteristics:
- High contrast — brilliant white against deep dark crema
- Thick, bold white pours
- Assertive tulips and rosettas
- Fast, aggressive pour technique
- Influenced by specialty coffee competition culture

### Sydney Style

Characteristics:
- Clean, precise symmetry
- Precision tulips with equal layers
- Fine, detailed rosettas
- Strong competition influence
- More restrained than Melbourne — quality over boldness

### Brisbane Style

Characteristics:
- Soft, rounded pours
- Balanced texture
- Smooth tulips with good layering
- Less aggressive than southern states

### Canberra Specialty Style

Characteristics:
- Technical, precise pours
- Fine-line work
- Strong balanced aesthetics
- Precision-focused — reflects the small but serious specialty coffee scene

---

## The Daily Training Standard

Australian specialty café baristas train daily. The standard:

Every shift before service:
- 10 hearts
- 10 tulips
- 10 rosettas

This is not optional. This is how skill is maintained.

---

## Training Priority Order

1. Milk texture — everything else depends on this
2. Hearts — foundation mechanics
3. Tulips — flow control and stacking
4. Rosettas — wiggle and backward movement
5. Swans — combination of all above

Do NOT skip the fundamentals. A barista who masters the heart has the mechanics for everything else. A barista who rushes to swans without mastering hearts builds on unstable foundations.

---

## Practical Assessment Criteria

To pass the Bean Culture latte art assessment, students must pour:

1. A heart
2. A 3-stack tulip
3. A rosetta
4. A swan

Judged on:

| Criterion | Description |
|---|---|
| Symmetry | Pattern is balanced, centred, equal on both sides |
| Contrast | Clear white-on-dark definition |
| Cleanliness | No stray bubbles, no smearing, clean lines |
| Texture | Milk quality is visibly correct |
| Centering | Pattern sits in the centre of the cup |
| Flow control | Evidence of deliberate speed changes where required |

Passing standard: Student demonstrates proper milk texture, correct pitcher control, correct cup angle, smooth movement, clean cut-throughs, and balanced symmetry across all four pours.

---

## Final Principle

> Latte art is not drawing. Latte art is fluid control.
>
> The best Australian café baristas are not simply making shapes. They are controlling flow, foam density, contrast, symmetry, timing, movement, and texture simultaneously.
>
> Great latte art should look effortless. The simpler the design appears, the more skill it usually required.
key_points: Melbourne = bold and high contrast; Sydney = precise and symmetrical; Brisbane = soft and balanced
Daily drill: 10 hearts, 10 tulips, 10 rosettas before every shift
Assessment: heart, 3-stack tulip, rosetta, and swan — judged on symmetry, contrast, and flow
Latte art is fluid control — not drawing

quiz.question: A student can pour consistent hearts and tulips but struggles with the rosetta. What is the correct training progression?
options: Skip the rosetta and move to the swan
Continue practising hearts and tulips, and add rosetta drills — the student is at the right stage
Go back to milk texturing practice only
Attempt competition pours to accelerate learning
quiz.explanation: Consistent hearts and tulips means the student has mastered the foundations. Rosetta is the correct next step. The training order is: milk texture → hearts → tulips → rosettas → swans. Each builds on the previous.

lessons.title: The Alternative Milk Landscape
lessons.content:
## The Alternative Milk Landscape

Alternative milks have gone from niche to mainstream. Understanding the major options helps you serve customers confidently and make better drink recommendations.

### Why Customers Choose Alternatives

- Dairy intolerance / lactose intolerance: Very common; lactase enzyme absent
- Milk allergy: Immune response to casein or whey proteins
- Vegan lifestyle: No animal products
- Environmental: Oat and soy have significantly lower carbon footprint than dairy
- Preference: Some simply prefer the flavour

### The Main Options

Oat milk
Creamy, mild, slightly sweet. Best for espresso drinks. Close to dairy in steaming behaviour.

Soy milk
Highest protein of plant milks. Can curdle when added to acidic espresso (soy-milk split). Better in lattes than flat whites.

Almond milk
Lighter, nuttier. Watery texture. Best for simple drinks. Low protein = poor foam.

Coconut milk
Rich, distinctive flavour. Can overpower delicate coffee. Works in flavoured drinks.

Macadamia milk
Smooth, buttery, premium. Growing in popularity at specialty cafés.

### The 'Split' Problem

Some plant milks curdle when poured into hot, acidic espresso. To prevent:
- Add espresso to milk (not the reverse)
- Use lower-acid coffees
- Heat the milk slightly before adding espresso
key_points: Oat milk is closest to dairy in behaviour
Soy can split in acidic espresso
Add espresso to milk to prevent curdling
Barista blends are formulated for better steaming

lessons.title: Steaming Alternative Milks
lessons.content:
## Steaming Alternative Milks

Each alternative milk has its own steaming personality. Success requires adapting your technique for each type.

### General Rules

1. Lower temperature: Most alternative milks steam best at 58–62°C, below the dairy target of 65°C
2. Less stretching: They foam more aggressively — introduce air briefly, then submerge
3. Faster service: Foam stability is lower — pour the drink within 15–20 seconds

### Oat Milk Technique

- Behaves most like dairy — use standard technique with slightly less stretching
- Steam to 60–62°C
- Produces smooth, pourable microfoam when using barista blends

### Soy Milk Technique

- Very sensitive to heat — watch temperature closely
- Steam to 60°C maximum
- Introduce air quickly, submerge early
- Don't re-steam under any circumstances — separates immediately

### Almond Milk Technique

- Hard to foam consistently — use barista blends only
- Minimal air, quick texture phase
- Expect less stable results — heart pour is more achievable than rosetta

### Coconut Milk

- High fat content can produce decent foam
- Strong flavour — better in drinks where this complements (chai latte, mocha)
- Steams to 60°C; avoid excessive stretching
key_points: Steam alt milks at 58–62°C, not the dairy 65°C target
Introduce air briefly, submerge quickly
Soy: maximum 60°C — very heat-sensitive
Pour immediately after steaming — foam degrades fast

quiz.question: At what temperature should most alternative milks be steamed?
quiz.explanation: Most alternative milks steam best at 58–62°C — slightly below the dairy target of 65°C. Their proteins and fats behave differently and break down faster at higher temperatures.

lessons.title: Menu Adaptation
lessons.content:
## Menu Adaptation

Offering alternative milks well means more than just having them available. The best cafés integrate them thoughtfully into the menu.

### Pairing with Coffee

Not all alternative milks suit all drinks equally:

| Drink | Best Alternative |
|---|---|
| Flat white | Oat (barista) |
| Latte | Oat or soy |
| Cappuccino | Oat or coconut |
| Iced latte | Almond or oat |
| Chai latte | Oat or coconut |
| Mocha | Any |

### Pricing

Alternative milks cost 2–4× more than dairy. A standard milk surcharge (typically $0.50–$1.00) is industry-accepted and helps offset this cost without penalising the customer.

### Cross-Contamination

- Keep dedicated jugs for each milk type
- Clearly label jugs
- Customers with nut allergies may react to almond or macadamia milk
- Oat is generally safe for nut allergies but not for celiacs (unless certified gluten-free oat)

### Customer Communication

When a customer asks 'what alternative milks do you have?' — know the answer confidently, and be able to advise which drinks work best with each option. This builds trust and upsells premium alternatives.
key_points: Oat barista milk suits most espresso drinks
A $0.50–$1.00 alt milk surcharge is standard
Keep dedicated and labelled jugs for each milk type
Be ready to advise customers on best milk pairings

lessons.title: Coffee Growing Regions
lessons.content:
## Coffee Growing Regions

Coffee grows in a band around the equator known as the 'Coffee Belt' — between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. Climate, altitude, and soil determine everything about the flavour in the cup.

### The Coffee Belt

Major producing regions:
- Africa: Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Burundi, Tanzania
- Central/South America: Colombia, Brazil, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Panama
- Asia/Pacific: Indonesia (Sumatra, Java), Papua New Guinea, Vietnam, India

### Africa

Ethiopia is the birthplace of coffee and produces some of the world's most prized lots. Expect bright acidity, blueberry, jasmine, bergamot, and tea-like complexity.

Kenya is known for its distinctive SL28 and SL34 varieties — blackcurrant, tomato, winey, intense acidity.

### Central & South America

Colombia's year-round harvest and diverse microclimates produce consistent, balanced coffees. Caramel, red apple, milk chocolate are common notes.

Brazil is the world's largest producer. Predominantly natural-processed, lower acid, nutty, chocolate, full-bodied.

### Asia Pacific

Indonesian coffees (Sumatra, Sulawesi) are earthy, full-bodied, low acid, with herbal and forest floor characteristics — very different from African or South American profiles.
key_points: Coffee grows in the equatorial 'Coffee Belt'
Ethiopia = birthplace of coffee, blueberry/floral notes
Kenya = blackcurrant and intense winey acidity
Brazil = world's largest producer, nutty and chocolatey

quiz.question: Which region is often described as the birthplace of coffee with blueberry and jasmine flavour notes?
quiz.explanation: Ethiopia is considered the birthplace of coffee and produces coffees prized for their blueberry, jasmine, bergamot, and tea-like complexity.

lessons.title: Altitude & Microclimate
lessons.content:
## Altitude & Microclimate

Altitude is one of the most important determinants of coffee quality. Higher altitude = slower cherry development = more complex flavour.

### Why Altitude Matters

At higher altitudes:
- Temperatures are cooler
- Coffee cherries develop more slowly (weeks or months longer)
- Slower development allows more complex sugars and acids to form
- Bean density increases — harder beans, better extraction

### Altitude Classifications

Many countries classify coffee by altitude:

| Classification | Altitude |
|---|---|
| High Grown (HG) | 1,200–1,500m |
| Strictly High Grown (SHG) | 1,500m+ |
| Strictly Hard Bean (SHB) | 1,200m+ (Guatemala/Costa Rica) |

### Microclimate

Altitude alone doesn't tell the full story. Microclimates — the specific combination of sun exposure, rainfall, wind, and soil at a specific farm or plot — create unique terroir.

Two farms at the same altitude in the same country can produce dramatically different coffee due to microclimate differences.

### Shade Growing

Shade-grown coffee (under forest canopy) further slows development and protects biodiversity. Many specialty producers use shade as a quality and sustainability tool.
key_points: Higher altitude = slower development = more complex flavour
SHG (Strictly High Grown) = 1,500m+
Microclimate creates terroir even within the same country
Shade growing slows development and improves quality

lessons.title: Varietals & Their Flavours
lessons.content:
## Varietals & Their Flavours

Just as wine has grape varieties (Shiraz, Riesling, Pinot Noir), coffee has varietals — each with distinct flavour characteristics.

### Key Arabica Varietals

Typica
The original Arabica variety. Clean, sweet, delicate. Parent of most other varieties.

Bourbon
A natural mutation of Typica found on the island of Réunion. Sweeter, more complex. Red Bourbon is most common; Yellow Bourbon (Brazil) is also prized.

Gesha/Geisha
Originating in Ethiopia, developed in Panama. Extraordinarily floral — jasmine, bergamot, tropical fruit. Commands some of the highest auction prices in the world.

SL28 / SL34
Developed in Kenya by Scott Laboratories. Produces the distinctive blackcurrant, tomato, and winey acidity Kenya is famous for.

Pacamara
A large-bean hybrid from El Salvador. Complex, intense, often with tropical fruit and fine acidity.

Catuai
A compact, high-yielding variety common in Brazil and Central America. Solid quality, good for commercial production.

### How Variety Affects Your Cup

The same variety grown in different regions will taste different. The same region growing different varieties will taste different. Both matter — this is why single-origin specialty coffee is always labelled with both.
key_points: Gesha = most prized varietal, jasmine and tropical fruit
Bourbon = sweeter and more complex than Typica
SL28/SL34 = Kenya's signature blackcurrant acidity
Both variety AND origin determine final cup flavour

lessons.title: Pour Over Methods
lessons.content:
## Pour Over Methods

Pour over is a manual, immersive brew method that gives the barista complete control over every variable. It's the best way to experience a coffee's full flavour potential.

### How It Works

Hot water is poured over coffee grounds in a filter. Gravity pulls the water through the grounds and filter into a vessel below. The filter removes oils and sediment, producing a clean, clear cup.

### Common Pour Over Devices

Hario V60
The most popular specialty device. Spiral ribs promote even flow. Requires skill to use well — flow rate and pour pattern matter significantly.

Chemex
Thicker paper filter removes more oils. Produces a very clean, clear cup. Excellent for showcasing origin characteristics.

Kalita Wave
Flat-bottom dripper with three small holes. More forgiving than V60. Even extraction due to flat bed.

Origami
Japanese design compatible with both cone and flat filters. Versatile and elegant.

### Basic Pour Over Recipe

- Ratio: 1:15 to 1:17 (coffee:water)
- Grind: Medium-coarse
- Temperature: 92–96°C
- Time: 3–4 minutes total

### The Bloom

Start with a 'bloom pour' — 2× the coffee weight in water. Wait 30–45 seconds. This allows CO2 to degas from fresh coffee, which would otherwise repel water and cause uneven extraction.
key_points: Pour over produces clean, clear cup with no sediment
Bloom pour degasses CO2 from fresh beans
V60 requires more skill; Kalita is more forgiving
Ratio: 1:15–1:17 for standard strength

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the 'bloom pour' in pour over brewing?
options: To allow CO2 to escape from fresh coffee
To add extra flavour to the brew
quiz.explanation: The bloom pour wets the grounds and allows CO2 gas to escape from freshly roasted coffee. If not degassed, CO2 repels water and causes uneven, channelled extraction.

lessons.title: AeroPress & Immersion
lessons.content:
## AeroPress & Immersion Brewing

Immersion brewing steeps coffee in water for a set time before separating the grounds. It's more forgiving than pour over and very versatile.

### AeroPress

The AeroPress is one of the most versatile and travel-friendly brew devices ever made. It uses immersion + pressure to brew a concentrated, smooth cup.

Standard Recipe:
- 15–17g coffee
- 200–220ml water at 80–85°C (lower temperature than most methods)
- Steep 1–2 minutes
- Press slowly over 20–30 seconds
- Dilute to taste, or drink as is

Inverted Method:
Flip the AeroPress upside down — allows longer steeping without dripping through the filter. Popular with specialty brewers.

World AeroPress Championship (WAC)
Yes — there is a World AeroPress Championship. Competitors submit recipes; judges taste blind. The winning recipe changes every year and reveals creative extremes possible with the device.

### French Press (Plunger)

Full immersion without any filter — coffee oils and fine particles remain in the cup. Produces full-bodied, rich, heavy cup. Very forgiving but requires coarse grind to avoid sludge.

### Cold Brew

Immersion of coarse-ground coffee in cold water for 12–24 hours. Produces a concentrate low in perceived acidity. Very different flavour profile from hot-brewed coffee.
key_points: AeroPress uses immersion + gentle pressure
Lower temperature (80–85°C) than most other methods
French press retains oils for heavier body
Cold brew: 12–24 hours steep, low perceived acidity

lessons.title: Matching Brew Method to Coffee
lessons.content:
## Matching Brew Method to Coffee

No single brew method is universally best — each method highlights different characteristics. Understanding this helps you recommend the right method for each coffee.

### The Matching Framework

Delicate, floral, fruity coffees (light roast Ethiopia, Kenya)
→ Best: V60, Chemex, Kalita Wave
→ Why: Clean filter removes oils; bright acidity and aroma shine through

Sweet, balanced coffees (medium roast Colombia, Guatemala)
→ Best: AeroPress, V60, Moka pot
→ Why: Versatile roast profiles suit most methods

Heavy, earthy coffees (dark roast Brazil, Sumatra)
→ Best: French press, cold brew, Moka pot
→ Why: Heavy body, low acidity suits immersion and metal filter methods

Espresso blends (medium-dark)
→ Best: Espresso machine, Moka pot
→ Why: Designed for high-pressure, short-extraction

### Grind and Method

| Method | Grind Size |
|---|---|
| Espresso | Very fine |
| Moka pot | Fine |
| AeroPress | Medium-fine |
| V60 / Kalita | Medium |
| French press | Coarse |
| Cold brew | Extra coarse |

### The Best Tool

The best brew method for any coffee is whichever one best highlights its strengths and minimises its weaknesses. There is no wrong answer — experimentation is always the right approach.
key_points: Light roast + pour over = clean, floral clarity
Heavy/earthy coffees suit French press and immersion
Grind size must match the brew method
Experimentation is always valid — taste decides

lessons.title: The Five Senses in Tasting
lessons.content:
## The Five Senses in Tasting Coffee

Coffee evaluation engages more senses than most people realise. Developing awareness of each creates a more complete sensory picture.

### Sight

Before you taste:
- Colour of the liquid (dark amber, golden, cloudy)
- Crema quality and colour (espresso)
- Clarity (filter coffee should be clear)
- Colour in the cup can hint at roast level and extraction

### Smell (Olfaction)

Aroma is the most powerful sense for flavour perception:
- Dry fragrance: Smell ground coffee before brewing — florals and fruit are most detectable here
- Wet aroma: Smell brewed coffee — caramel, chocolate, and roast notes emerge with heat
- Retronasal aroma: Aroma experienced through the back of the nose while tasting — responsible for most of what we call 'flavour'

### Taste

Your tongue detects five basic tastes:
- Sweet — front of tongue
- Sour — sides
- Bitter — back of tongue
- Salty — distributed
- Umami — present in aged and fermented coffees

### Touch (Mouthfeel/Body)

Physical sensation in the mouth — weight, viscosity, coating, astringency.

### Hearing

Less obvious but real — the sound of grinding, the crackle of roasting, and even the pour influence perception and anticipation.
key_points: Aroma accounts for most of what we perceive as flavour
Dry fragrance and wet aroma reveal different compounds
Tongue detects sweet, sour, bitter, salty, umami
Body is a tactile/physical sensation, not a taste

quiz.question: What is retronasal aroma?
options: The smell of coffee beans before grinding
Aroma experienced through the back of the nose while tasting
The smell of freshly brewed coffee from the top of the cup
Aroma released when hot water contacts coffee
quiz.explanation: Retronasal aroma is the smell experienced through the back of the nasal passage while tasting. It is the primary mechanism by which we experience what we call 'flavour' in food and drink.

lessons.title: Identifying Off-Flavours
lessons.content:
## Identifying Off-Flavours

Off-flavours are undesirable tastes and aromas that indicate a problem — with the beans, the roast, the equipment, or the brew. Learning to identify them is essential for quality control.

### Common Off-Flavours

Staleness / Papery / Cardboard
Cause: Old coffee, or oxidised oils from poor storage.
Fix: Use fresher beans, store correctly in sealed container away from light.

Rubber / Chemical / Medicinal
Cause: Equipment contamination, cleaning chemical residue, or robusta-heavy blend.
Fix: Thorough cleaning and rinsing; check bean source.

Mouldy / Earthy (not intentional)
Cause: Defective beans (mould during drying), or water contamination.
Fix: Source better quality beans; check water supply.

Metallic
Cause: Scale inside machine, or very low TDS water that leaches metals.
Fix: Descale machine; adjust water mineral content.

Rancid / Soapy
Cause: Old coffee oils. Occurs in unclean equipment or very stale beans.
Fix: Clean group head, baskets, and grinder thoroughly.

Phenolic / Medicinal
Cause: Bacterial contamination in fermentation (processing defect).
Fix: Source quality beans with clean fermentation.

### Tasting Reference

Intentionally tasting defective coffee (old beans, bad shots) is the fastest way to calibrate your palate to off-flavours. Know what bad tastes like so you can always prevent it.
key_points: Papery = stale beans or oxidised oils
Metallic = scale buildup or low-mineral water
Rancid/soapy = old oils in unclean equipment
Intentionally taste defects to calibrate your palate

lessons.title: Sensory Training Exercises
lessons.content:
## Sensory Training Exercises

A skilled palate is built through deliberate, consistent practice. These exercises are used by competition baristas and Q Graders worldwide.

### Exercise 1: Triangle Test

Present three cups: two the same, one different. Identify the odd one out.
This trains ability to detect subtle differences.

### Exercise 2: Descriptive Tasting

Taste a coffee blind and write 3–5 descriptors before checking the roaster's tasting notes. Compare your notes to the roaster's.
Objective: Reduce gap between your perception and trained perception.

### Exercise 3: Acid Identification

Prepare very dilute solutions of citric acid (lemon), malic acid (apple), and acetic acid (vinegar). Taste each blind.
Objective: Learn to identify acid types in coffee.

### Exercise 4: Intensity Calibration

Pull shots at 15%, 20%, and 25% extraction. Taste all three.
Objective: Understand what under, correct, and over-extraction tastes like for THIS specific coffee.

### Exercise 5: Aroma Kit

La Nez du Café (the coffee nose) is a set of 36 aromas in vials. Smell each blind and guess.
Objective: Build aroma vocabulary and recognition.

### Building a Habit

Taste intentionally every day. Even a simple walk through the flavour wheel for your morning coffee trains your brain to categorise what it perceives.
key_points: Triangle tests train detection of subtle differences
Blind tasting then comparing to roaster notes builds vocabulary
Acid identification helps diagnose extraction issues
Daily intentional tasting compounds rapidly over weeks

lessons.title: What Is Cupping?
lessons.content:
## What Is Cupping?

Cupping is the standardised professional method for evaluating coffee. It's used by roasters, buyers, Q Graders, and producers worldwide to assess quality, compare lots, and make purchasing decisions.

### Why Cupping?

Cupping removes the variables of brewing equipment and technique. Everyone evaluates the same coffee prepared the same way, making it possible to compare results across labs and countries.

### SCA Cupping Protocol (Overview)

1. Weigh: 8.25g per 150ml water (approximately 1:18.18 ratio)
2. Grind: Medium-coarse (slightly coarser than filter)
3. Evaluate dry fragrance: Smell grounds before adding water
4. Add water: 93°C, poured to saturate all grounds, timed start
5. Evaluate wet aroma: Smell the crust after 4 minutes
6. Break the crust: Push the crust down with a spoon at 4 minutes, smell the released aroma
7. Skim and clean: Remove foam and floating grounds
8. Taste: Begin at approximately 11 minutes (when temperature reaches ~71°C)
9. Score: Rate on SCA form

### The SCA Cupping Form

Coffees are scored across 10 attributes, each up to 10 points. Defects are subtracted. The maximum score is 100.

Coffees scoring 80+ are classified as Specialty Coffee.
key_points: Cupping = standardised evaluation method, removes brewer variables
SCA ratio: 8.25g per 150ml
Break the crust at 4 minutes and evaluate aroma
80+ SCA score = Specialty Coffee classification

quiz.question: What SCA score threshold qualifies a coffee as 'Specialty Coffee'?
quiz.explanation: Coffees scoring 80 or above on the SCA cupping form are classified as Specialty Coffee. Below 80 is considered commodity grade.

lessons.title: The SCA Scoring System
lessons.content:
## The SCA Scoring System

The SCA cupping form scores coffee across 10 attributes, each rated from 6–10 points in 0.25 increments. Understanding each attribute makes you a more precise evaluator.

### The 10 Attributes

1. Fragrance/Aroma — dry grounds + wet aroma after water is added
2. Flavour — overall impression of the coffee from first sip
3. Aftertaste — length and quality of the finish
4. Acidity — quality and intensity; described as bright, lively, or harsh
5. Body — weight and texture in the mouth
6. Balance — how well all attributes work together
7. Sweetness — presence of pleasant sweetness (natural, not added)
8. Uniformity — consistency across all five cups of the same coffee
9. Clean Cup — absence of off-flavours or taints in any cup
10. Overall — the holistic impression; personal/subjective score

### Defect Scoring

Category 1 defects (e.g. phenolic, sour, rotten): subtract 4 points per cup affected
Category 2 defects (e.g. medicinal, rubber, musty): subtract 2 points per cup

### Score Ranges

| Score | Classification |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | Outstanding |
| 85–89.99 | Excellent |
| 80–84.99 | Very Good (Specialty) |
| Below 80 | Not Specialty |

### Q Graders

A Q Grader is a licensed coffee professional who has passed a rigorous multi-day examination to certify their ability to use the SCA system accurately and consistently.
key_points: 10 attributes scored 6–10 each
Clean Cup and Uniformity are scored across all 5 cups
Category 1 defects subtract 4 points, Category 2 subtract 2
Q Grader certification requires passing a rigorous multi-day exam

lessons.title: Running a Cupping Session
lessons.content:
## Running a Cupping Session

Knowing the protocol is one thing — running a smooth, useful cupping session takes practice and preparation.

### Setup

- Prepare 5 cups per coffee (SCA standard for statistical reliability)
- Use identical cups (ideally 200–250ml ceramic cupping bowls)
- Same grinder setting for all samples — grind as close to cupping as possible
- Label cups face-down to prevent bias during cupping
- Provide spittoons — professional cuppers spit during evaluation (like wine tasting)

### Running the Session

1. Dry fragrance: All participants smell dry grounds, take notes
2. Add water simultaneously — use a consistent pouring pattern to ensure equal steep time
3. Wet aroma at 4 minutes — evaluate and note before breaking
4. Break at 4 minutes — everyone breaks simultaneously
5. Taste from ~11 minutes — slurp loudly
6. Evaluate as cooling — different characteristics emerge at different temperatures
7. Score independently — no discussion until all have scored
8. Discuss discrepancies — most valuable part of a group cupping

### Blind vs Open Cupping

- Blind cupping: Samples are unknown. Reduces bias. Best for QC and purchasing decisions.
- Open cupping: Samples are identified. Better for learning and discussing origins.

### Using Cupping Data

Track scores over time to: identify batch consistency, compare roast profiles, select lots for purchase, and benchmark your own palate calibration.
key_points: Cup 5 samples per coffee for statistical reliability
Evaluate dry fragrance, then wet aroma, then taste
Score independently before discussing with others
Blind cupping removes bias; open cupping is better for learning

lessons.title: Green Bean to Roasted Bean
lessons.content:
## Green Bean to Roasted Bean

The roasting process transforms a dense, pale green seed into the aromatic, complex bean we grind and brew. Understanding this transformation is the foundation of roasting knowledge.

### Green Coffee

Green coffee beans are:
- Pale green, dense, and hard
- Smell grassy, hay-like, or vegetable-like
- High in moisture (10–12%)
- Contain all the precursors for flavour but none of the flavour itself

### Stages of Roasting

1. Drying Phase (0–5 min, up to 150°C)
Moisture evaporates. The bean turns from green to yellow. Endothermic process — bean absorbs heat.

2. Yellowing (150–170°C)
The Maillard reaction begins — amino acids and sugars react to create hundreds of new aromatic compounds. Colour turns yellow, then light brown.

3. First Crack (196°C)
Steam and CO2 cause the bean to expand and crack audibly — like popcorn. This is when light roast coffees can be dropped. The bean becomes exothermic (releases heat).

4. Development (post first crack)
Flavour develops rapidly. The roaster has the most control here. Drop time determines roast level.

5. Second Crack (224°C)
Cell walls fracture — oils emerge to the surface. Dark roasts are taken into or beyond this stage. Increasingly bitter, smoky, bold.

### The Maillard Reaction

The Maillard reaction is the most important chemical process in roasting. It creates thousands of flavour-active compounds including caramels, melanoidins, and aromatic molecules responsible for coffee's complexity.
key_points: Green beans are pale, dense, and smell grassy
First crack (196°C) marks transition to light roast
The Maillard reaction creates hundreds of flavour compounds
Second crack (~224°C) marks dark roast territory

quiz.question: At what temperature does 'first crack' typically occur during roasting?
quiz.explanation: First crack typically occurs around 196°C. This is when steam and CO2 cause the bean to expand and crack audibly — the minimum point for a drinkable roast.

lessons.title: Roast Equipment
lessons.content:
## Roast Equipment

Roasters come in many types and sizes. Understanding the equipment helps you understand roast profiles and quality control.

### Drum Roasters

The most common commercial roaster type. Beans tumble inside a rotating drum while heat is applied externally (gas flame) or convectively (hot air).

- Small-batch (1–3kg): Specialty roasters, sample roasting, micro-roasters
- Production (5–120kg): Commercial roasters, high-volume production

Famous brands: Probat, Giesen, Loring, Diedrich, Joper

### Fluid Bed (Air) Roasters

Hot air suspends and roasts the beans simultaneously. Very fast and even roast. Less development of body and complexity vs drum. Popular for home and small commercial use.

Famous brands: Behmor, Aillio Bullet (hybrid)

### Sample Roasters

Tiny roasters (50–250g) used to evaluate green coffee before committing to a large purchase. Quick, consistent, essential tool for sourcing.

### Key Measurements

- Charge temperature: Temperature of the drum when beans are loaded
- Turning point: When bean temperature stops falling and starts rising after loading
- ROR (Rate of Rise): How fast the bean temperature is increasing — the most important roasting metric
- Development Time Ratio (DTR): Time from first crack to drop ÷ total roast time. Typically 20–25%.
key_points: Drum roasters are most common commercial type
Rate of Rise (ROR) is the most important roasting metric
DTR = development time ÷ total roast time, target 20–25%
Sample roasters evaluate green coffee before purchase

lessons.title: Roast Level & Flavour Impact
lessons.content:
## Roast Level & Flavour Impact

Roast level is the most visible quality of a coffee — but its impact on flavour goes far deeper than colour.

### Light Roast

- Drop at or just after first crack (196–205°C)
- Retains most origin character — fruity, floral, acidic
- Higher perceived acidity
- Denser bean — harder to grind and extract
- Shorter shelf life than dark (higher moisture retention)

### Medium Roast

- Dropped 1–3 minutes after first crack (205–215°C)
- Balance of origin character and roast flavour
- Caramel, chocolate, nutty notes emerge
- Most versatile for different brew methods
- Most popular commercially

### Dark Roast

- Dropped into or beyond second crack (~218°C+)
- Roast flavours dominate — smoky, bitter, oily
- Low acidity, heavy body
- Origin characteristics largely masked
- Oils on bean surface — extracts easily and quickly

### Colour Measurement

Roasters use a Colorette or Agtron meter to measure roast colour objectively in Agtron units:
- Light: 70+ Agtron
- Medium: 55–70 Agtron
- Dark: Below 45 Agtron

### The Roaster's Art

A great roaster highlights each coffee's best qualities. Light roast is not inherently better than dark — the goal is to roast each coffee to express its potential, not to chase a trend.
key_points: Light roast = origin character, high acidity, dense bean
Medium roast = balance of origin and roast flavours
Dark roast = roast flavours dominate, low acidity
Agtron units measure roast colour objectively

lessons.title: Reading a Roast Profile
lessons.content:
## Reading a Roast Profile

A roast profile is a graph showing bean temperature over time during a roast. Reading profiles is the primary skill of a professional roaster.

### The Axes

- X-axis: Time (minutes)
- Y-axis: Temperature (°C)
- Secondary line: Rate of Rise (ROR) — how fast temperature is climbing per unit of time

### Key Points on the Curve

Charge: Point where beans enter the drum. Temperature usually drops briefly.
Turning Point: The lowest point on the curve (30–60s in). Bean temperature stops dropping and begins to rise.
Maillard Onset (150°C): Colour change begins, aromatic development starts.
First Crack: Audible, visible on the profile as a brief ROR drop.
Development: Time between first crack and drop.
Drop: End of roast.

### Rate of Rise (ROR)

ROR is the most important roasting metric:
- Too fast ROR = baked flavours (flat, dull)
- Declining ROR through the roast is ideal (start fast, slow down progressively)
- ROR crash (rapid decline) near the end can cause tipping or scorching
- Flat ROR = stalled roast → baked, empty flavour

### Software Tools

Roasters use software like Cropster, Artisan, or Mill City to log and visualise profiles in real time. This allows precise replication and diagnosis of problems.
key_points: Roast profile = bean temperature vs time graph
Rate of Rise (ROR) should decline progressively through the roast
A crashing ROR causes tipping; a flat ROR causes baked flavours
Software like Artisan logs profiles for analysis and replication

quiz.question: What does a 'stalled' or flat Rate of Rise (ROR) typically indicate in a roast?
options: The beans are about to crack
The roast may produce baked, flat, dull flavours
The drum temperature is too high
quiz.explanation: A flat ROR means the bean temperature is no longer climbing — the roast has stalled. This typically results in baked, dull, flat flavours with a lack of sweetness and complexity.

lessons.title: Designing a Roast Profile
lessons.content:
## Designing a Roast Profile

Creating a roast profile isn't random — it's a deliberate design process that considers the coffee's origin, density, moisture content, and desired flavour outcome.

### Starting Points

Charge temperature
- Higher charge = more initial heat, faster drying phase
- Lower charge = slower, more gentle drying — good for dense, high-altitude beans

Gas/heat input
- Controls how fast ROR climbs
- Most roasters apply high heat at charge, then progressively reduce

Airflow
- Controls how quickly heat is removed from the drum
- More airflow = faster heat removal = lower ROR
- Critical for development — too little airflow traps chaff and smoke

### The Three-Phase Framework

1. Drying phase: Drive off moisture quickly but not so fast it scorches the exterior. Target: first crack in no less than 8 minutes.
2. Maillard/browning phase: Maillard reaction builds flavour. Moderate ROR, controlled development.
3. Development phase: From first crack to drop. Typically 20–25% of total roast time. Controls sweetness and complexity.

### DTR (Development Time Ratio)

DTR = (Time from first crack to drop) ÷ (Total roast time)

Target DTR for most coffees: 20–25%
- Under 20%: Underdeveloped, grassy, lacking sweetness
- Over 30%: Baked, flat, diminishing origin character
key_points: Charge temperature sets the initial heat load
Airflow controls heat removal and chaff evacuation
DTR of 20–25% is the development target for most coffees
Total roast under 8 minutes risks scorching before first crack

lessons.title: Replicating & Iterating
lessons.content:
## Replicating & Iterating Roast Profiles

A great roast profile is only valuable if you can replicate it. And replication is only possible with precise records and consistent technique.

### The Replication Challenge

Multiple variables change between roasts:
- Ambient temperature — affects drum behaviour
- Humidity — affects bean moisture
- Green bean batch variation — even the same lot varies slightly
- Gas pressure — can vary with supply

### Logging Every Roast

Record for every roast:
- Date and time
- Ambient temp and humidity
- Green bean batch code and moisture content
- Charge temperature
- All milestones (turning point, first crack, drop)
- Drum speed, gas setting, airflow at each point
- Tasting notes from the sample roast

### Iterating Toward a Target

When adjusting a profile:
1. Define the target (e.g. 'more sweetness, less brightness')
2. Form a hypothesis (e.g. 'extend development time by 15 seconds')
3. Change ONE variable
4. Cup the result blind
5. Compare to previous roast
6. Record results and repeat

### Batch Consistency

Professional roasters cup every batch — a sample from every production roast is cupped within 24 hours to check for consistency, defects, or unexpected variation. Any batch outside the acceptable range is re-roasted or rejected.
key_points: Log ambient conditions, milestones, and settings every roast
Change one variable at a time when iterating
Cup every batch within 24 hours of roasting
Ambient conditions affect replication — control for them

lessons.title: Green Coffee Defects
lessons.content:
## Green Coffee Defects

Defects in green coffee are physical or biological problems that affect the final cup. Sorting and grading at origin reduces defects, but roasters must also screen incoming lots.

### Primary (Category 1) Defects

These cause the most damage to flavour:
- Full black bean: Fermented, phenolic, rotten taste
- Full sour: Acetic acid, vinegary off-flavour
- Dried cherry / pod: Can introduce fermented/fruity defects
- Fungus damaged: Mouldy, musty, phenolic
- Foreign matter: Rocks, sticks, other non-coffee material

Allowable rate in specialty coffee: Maximum 0 full defects per 350g sample

### Secondary (Category 2) Defects

Less severe but still impactful:
- Partial black / sour
- Parchment left on bean
- Insect damage (coffee borer holes)
- Floaters (underdeveloped, hollow beans)
- Shell / elephant bean (abnormal structure)

Allowable rate in specialty: Maximum 5 defects per 350g sample

### Sorting Methods

- Optical sorters: Machine vision systems that detect colour and shape defects at high speed
- Hand sorting: Labour-intensive but catches what machines miss
- Density sorting: Separates beans by weight — floaters and defects are lighter
- Water flotation: Defective beans float; dense healthy beans sink
key_points: Category 1 defects: zero allowed in specialty grade
Black beans and sours cause the most flavour damage
Optical sorters detect colour defects at high speed
Floaters are underdeveloped and hollow — they burn in the roaster

lessons.title: Post-Roast Quality Checks
lessons.content:
## Post-Roast Quality Checks

A roast is only as good as the quality check that follows it. Even an expert roaster can produce a subpar batch — systematic checking catches problems before they reach the customer.

### Colour Measurement

Use an Agtron meter or Colorette to measure roast colour on a ground sample. Compare to the target Agtron value for this coffee.

If the colour is outside ±2 Agtron units of target → investigate cause before next roast.

### Moisture Loss

Weigh green coffee before roasting and compare to weight after roasting. Typical moisture loss = 14–20% (weight loss).

- Under 14% → likely underdeveloped
- Over 20% → likely over-roasted

### Sample Cupping

Cup within 24–48 hours of roasting (after the beans have off-gassed briefly):
- Assess for defects, off-flavours, and consistency
- Compare to the approved profile cup
- Score on the SCA form

### Batch Rejection Criteria

Define your rejection criteria in advance:
- More than 1 Category 1 defect per 350g
- SCA score below minimum threshold
- Colour more than 3 Agtron units from target
- Unacceptable off-flavour in cupping

### Customer Feedback Loop

Encourage feedback from customers and wholesale partners. First-hand reports of unusual flavour are valuable QC data that your internal checks may miss.
key_points: Measure roast colour with Agtron within target range
Moisture loss should be 14–20%
Cup every batch within 24–48 hours of roasting
Define rejection criteria in advance — don't make exceptions

quiz.question: What typical weight-loss percentage should you expect from roasting green coffee?
quiz.explanation: Roasting typically causes 14–20% weight loss due to moisture evaporation and the release of CO2. Less than 14% suggests underdevelopment; more than 20% suggests over-roasting.

lessons.title: Storage & Freshness
lessons.content:
## Storage & Freshness

Even perfectly roasted coffee deteriorates rapidly without correct storage. Understanding and controlling freshness is a critical part of quality management.

### What Causes Staleness

Oxidation: Oxygen reacts with coffee oils and aromatic compounds, producing rancid, cardboard-like off-flavours.

CO2 off-gassing: Freshly roasted coffee releases CO2 for days to weeks. This is why whole bean coffee bags have one-way valves (not two-way) — releasing CO2 without letting oxygen in.

Moisture absorption: Coffee is hygroscopic — it absorbs ambient moisture, which accelerates oxidation and alters grind.

Light: UV light degrades aromatic compounds.

Heat: Accelerates all of the above.

### Optimal Storage

- Whole bean: Sealed bag with one-way valve, room temperature, dark location
- Ground coffee: Oxidises 5× faster than whole bean — only grind what you need
- Refrigerator: Not recommended (moisture and odour absorption)
- Freezer: Acceptable for long-term storage if beans are airtight and frozen in one portion (never refreeze)

### Freshness Windows

| Coffee Type | Peak Freshness | Acceptable |
|---|---|---|
| Espresso | 7–21 days from roast | Up to 4 weeks |
| Filter | 7–30 days from roast | Up to 6 weeks |
| After grinding | 15–30 minutes | Up to 2 hours |

### Communicating Freshness

All specialty roasters date their bags with a roast date. Teach customers to prioritise roast date over best-before date.
key_points: Oxygen, moisture, light, and heat all degrade coffee
One-way valve bags release CO2 without letting oxygen in
Ground coffee oxidises 5× faster than whole bean
Never store in the refrigerator — moisture and odour absorption

lessons.title: Building a Drinks Menu
lessons.content:
## Building a Drinks Menu

A drinks menu is more than a list — it's a statement of identity, a sales tool, and a reflection of your bar's skill level. Building one thoughtfully separates great cafés from average ones.

### Start with the Coffee

Every menu decision flows from the coffee you're serving:
- What are the flavour characteristics of your espresso blend?
- Does it suit a 1:2 ratio or does it shine at 1:2.5?
- What milk temperature and texture does it need?

### Core Menu vs Signature Drinks

Core menu: Espresso, long black, flat white, latte, cappuccino, cold brew. These are expected by every customer.

Signature drinks: 1–3 unique creations that reflect your identity. These justify premium pricing and create talking points.

### Designing Signature Drinks

1. Start with a flavour concept (e.g. 'a coffee with the mood of a pine forest')
2. Select ingredients that complement the coffee — avoid competing with it
3. Develop a recipe with precise measurements
4. Test extensively — 20+ iterations if needed
5. Train staff until the drink is executed perfectly by everyone

### Pricing

- Use a costing sheet: ingredients + labour + overhead + margin
- Food cost target: 25–35% of sale price for drinks
- Signature drinks can carry a premium: signal quality, not gouging

### Seasonal Menu Updates

Rotating 1–2 seasonal specials keeps regulars engaged and showcases new ingredients. Tie to local seasons or coffee harvest cycles.
key_points: Core menu sets the baseline; signature drinks build identity
All menu decisions flow from the coffee's flavour profile
Drink COGS target: 25–35% of sale price
Seasonal specials keep regulars engaged and signal freshness

lessons.title: Costing & Margins
lessons.content:
## Costing & Margins

Every drink on your menu either builds or erodes your business. Understanding cost structure is not just accounting — it's craft knowledge.

### Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)

For a flat white:
- 19g espresso blend @ $0.08/g = $1.52
- 160ml whole milk @ $0.003/ml = $0.48
- Cup (if takeaway) = $0.18
- Lid = $0.05
- Total COGS = $2.23

If the flat white sells for $6.50:
COGS% = 2.23 / 6.50 = 34%

### The Pricing Formula

Sale price = COGS ÷ target food cost %

If your target COGS is 30%: $2.23 ÷ 0.30 = $7.43 minimum price

### Labour and Overhead

COGS covers ingredients only. Your total cost per drink must also account for:
- Barista labour (hourly rate ÷ drinks per hour)
- Rent (per transaction)
- Utilities, equipment, marketing

A well-run café typically operates at 30–35% COGS and 28–35% labour, leaving 15–25% for rent, overhead, and profit.

### Waste Control

Milk waste is the biggest controllable cost in espresso bars:
- Track milk usage vs sales
- Set pour standards (exact jug sizes)
- Train staff to not over-pour or discard usable milk

A 10% reduction in milk waste on a busy café can save thousands per year.
key_points: Track COGS for every drink on the menu
Target COGS: 25–35% of sale price
Labour and overhead are separate from COGS but equally important
Milk waste is the highest-value controllable cost in a coffee bar

quiz.question: If a drink costs $2.50 to make and you want a 30% food cost, what should the minimum sale price be?
quiz.explanation: Sale price = COGS ÷ target food cost % = $2.50 ÷ 0.30 = $8.33. This ensures your ingredient cost is 30% of what the customer pays.

lessons.title: Seasonal & Specialty Drinks
lessons.content:
## Seasonal & Specialty Drinks

Seasonal and specialty drinks are some of the most powerful tools in a café's arsenal — they drive excitement, social media attention, and new customer visits.

### Why Seasonal Specials Work

- Urgency: Limited availability drives FOMO
- Novelty: Regulars have a reason to visit
- Social sharing: Unique drinks get photographed and posted
- Storytelling: Every special has a story — tell it on the board and to customers

### Developing a Seasonal Special

1. Identify the seasonal ingredient: Stone fruit in summer, warming spices in winter, citrus in autumn
2. Choose the coffee base: What espresso style suits the ingredient?
3. Develop the recipe: Start simple. Complexity can be added later.
4. Name it well: Evocative names outperform descriptive names ('Ember' sells better than 'Salted Caramel Espresso')
5. Brief your team: Everyone serves it with the same story

### Examples by Season

Summer: Cold brew lemonade, coconut cold brew, sparkling espresso tonic
Autumn: Apple and cardamom latte, fig and hazelnut flat white
Winter: Spiced orange espresso, salted caramel oat latte
Spring: Elderflower latte, lavender honey flat white

### Measurement & Recipe Cards

Every special must have a recipe card with gram-precise measurements. Consistency is the difference between a special that becomes iconic and one that customers never reorder.
key_points: Limited availability creates urgency and repeat visits
Evocative names outperform descriptive names
Every seasonal special needs a precise recipe card
Brief your entire team so the story is told consistently

lessons.title: Adult Learning Principles
lessons.content:
## Adult Learning Principles

Teaching barista skills is different from teaching children in school. Adults learn differently — understanding how helps you train more effectively.

### The ARCS Model of Motivation

Attention: Capture interest first. A boring demo loses the learner immediately.
Relevance: Connect skills to the trainee's real goals ('this will make your shifts easier').
Confidence: Set achievable milestones. Early wins build motivation.
Satisfaction: Provide genuine positive reinforcement when earned.

### The 70/20/10 Rule

Adult learning breaks down approximately as:
- 70% from doing (on-the-job practice)
- 20% from feedback (coaching, observation)
- 10% from formal training (classroom, videos)

This means most of your training impact happens during service, not in a training session.

### Demonstration Before Practice

Always demonstrate before asking someone to try:
1. Explain what you're about to do (the 'why')
2. Demonstrate at full speed
3. Demonstrate slowly with commentary
4. Have the trainee try
5. Give specific feedback
6. Repeat steps 4–5

### Psychological Safety

Trainees learn faster when they feel safe to make mistakes. Create a culture where pulling a bad shot is a learning opportunity, not an embarrassment.
key_points: Adults need relevance — connect training to their goals
70% of adult learning comes from doing, not instruction
Always demonstrate before asking someone to practice
Psychological safety accelerates learning significantly

lessons.title: Structuring a Training Plan
lessons.content:
## Structuring a Training Plan

A training plan without structure is just a list of things to do. A well-structured plan moves trainees through progressive complexity with clear milestones.

### The Three-Phase Structure

Phase 1: Foundation (Week 1)
- Coffee knowledge basics
- Equipment familiarity and safety
- Observation: Watch experienced baristas, no hands on equipment yet
- Basic cleaning and maintenance routines

Phase 2: Skills Development (Week 2–3)
- Supervised espresso pulling: grind, dose, distribute, tamp, extract
- Milk steaming: warm jugs, basic stretch and texture
- Basic pours: simple latte, flat white, cappuccino
- Supervised service at quieter periods

Phase 3: Consolidation (Week 4+)
- Increasing complexity and speed
- Latte art introduction (heart, then tulip)
- Peak hour service with support
- Problem-solving: what to do when things go wrong

### Competency Checklists

For each skill, define what 'competent' looks like:
- Espresso: Shot within recipe (dose, yield, time) on 3 consecutive attempts
- Milk: No visible bubbles, 60–65°C, pourable texture, 3 consecutive
- Latte art: Recognisable heart on 3 consecutive pours

### Sign-Off Process

Have a second senior barista or trainer sign off each competency independently. This maintains standards and gives the trainee external validation.
key_points: Three phases: Foundation → Skills → Consolidation
Define 'competent' in observable, measurable terms
Require 3 consecutive successful attempts for sign-off
Independent sign-off maintains standards and motivates trainees

lessons.title: Giving Effective Feedback
lessons.content:
## Giving Effective Feedback

Feedback is the most powerful training tool — and the most misused. Learning to give precise, timely, constructive feedback will make you an exceptional trainer.

### The SBI Model

Situation: Describe the specific situation
Behaviour: Describe the specific behaviour you observed
Impact: Describe the impact of that behaviour

Example: 'When you tamped just now (S), I noticed the tamp was angled to the left (B) — that caused the shot to channel and run unevenly on one side (I).'

### Avoid Vague Feedback

- Bad: 'Good job!'
- Good: 'The milk texture was perfect — glossy, no bubbles, and the temperature was right on 63°C.'

- Bad: 'That wasn't great.'
- Good: 'The shot ran in 18 seconds — that's too fast, and you can taste it (sour). Let's grind two steps finer.'

### Timing

- Give feedback immediately or within minutes — not hours later
- In a busy service, note issues and debrief after the rush
- During training sessions, give real-time coaching

### Positive Reinforcement

Recognise improvements specifically and sincerely:
- 'Your distribution is much more even than last week — the shots are extracting more consistently now.'

### When Trainers Disagree

If you're coaching and the trainee has developed a different technique that still works — evaluate objectively. If results are good, the technique may be valid. Standards matter; dogma doesn't.
key_points: Use SBI model: Situation, Behaviour, Impact
Vague praise is unhelpful — be specific
Give feedback immediately or during debrief, never hours later
Recognise improvement specifically to reinforce positive behaviour

quiz.question: What does the 'B' in the SBI feedback model stand for?
quiz.explanation: SBI stands for Situation, Behaviour, Impact. The Behaviour component describes the specific observable action you noticed — making the feedback concrete and actionable.

lessons.title: Café Economics
lessons.content:
## Café Economics

Understanding how a café makes (and loses) money is essential knowledge for anyone who wants to run one — or help one succeed.

### Revenue Streams

- Coffee drinks: Highest margin per item, highest volume
- Food: Lower margin, higher COGS, essential for average spend
- Retail: Coffee beans, merchandise — high margin, low volume
- Wholesale: Selling beans to other cafés or offices

### The Cost Structure

A café's costs broadly break down as:

| Cost | Target % of Revenue |
|---|---|
| Cost of Goods Sold (food & drink) | 28–35% |
| Labour | 28–35% |
| Rent | 8–15% |
| Other overheads | 10–15% |
| Net profit | 5–15% |

### Average Transaction Value (ATV)

ATV = total revenue ÷ number of transactions

Increasing ATV is one of the highest-leverage actions:
- Add food to every coffee order
- Offer size upgrades
- Promote retail beans
- Train staff to upsell naturally, not pushily

### Covers Per Hour

A busy espresso bar might serve 50–80 covers per hour. Knowing your peak capacity and actual throughput helps identify bottlenecks — usually grind, milk, or staffing.

### Break-Even Analysis

Knowing your fixed costs (rent + salaries) and contribution margin (sale price minus variable cost per item) lets you calculate exactly how many coffees per day you need to sell to break even.
key_points: Coffee drinks are highest-margin, highest-volume item
Labour and COGS together target 56–70% of revenue
ATV increase is highest-leverage growth lever
Know your break-even number in coffees per day

lessons.title: Waste & Efficiency
lessons.content:
## Waste & Efficiency

In a café, waste is the silent profit killer. Identifying and reducing waste in all its forms can significantly improve profitability without changing prices.

### Types of Waste

Milk waste
The most significant controllable cost. Every jug of milk poured and not used costs money.
- Track milk per shift vs drinks sold
- Set exact jug sizes per drink type
- Train staff to not overpour or discard warm milk unnecessarily

Coffee waste
Dialling in, dead shots, rejected drinks:
- Track grams of coffee ground vs coffee sold
- Efficient dialling in = fewer wasted shots
- Dead shots from a grinder left on = preventable waste

Food waste
The biggest percentage waste in most cafés:
- Order to par (daily order matched to projected sales)
- FIFO (First In First Out) stock rotation
- Sell-by-end-of-day specials

Time waste
Inefficient workflow, poor station setup, waiting:
- Station must be set up before service
- Everything within arm's reach
- Eliminate backtracking

### Workflow Design

The espresso station should flow logically:
Grinder → portafilter → group head → milk station → cup → customer

Every unnecessary step = seconds per drink × hundreds of drinks per day = significant time cost.
key_points: Milk waste is the highest-value controllable cost
Track grams of coffee ground vs drinks sold
FIFO stock rotation reduces food waste
Efficient station layout eliminates time waste across hundreds of drinks

lessons.title: Customer Experience & Retention
lessons.content:
## Customer Experience and Service

The best marketing any café can do is making every customer want to come back. Retention is cheaper, more reliable, and more valuable than acquisition.

### The Experience Beyond the Coffee

Customers return for more than coffee — they return for how a place makes them feel:
- Welcome: Were they acknowledged when they walked in?
- Speed: Was the wait appropriate for the situation?
- Consistency: Was the coffee as good as last time?
- Care: Did staff remember their order?

### The Regular Effect

Regulars represent disproportionate revenue. A customer who visits 4×/week spends 4× more than one who visits weekly — and they bring friends.

Invest in remembering regulars:
- Learn names
- Remember orders
- Notice and acknowledge changes ('haven't seen you in a while')

### Handling Complaints

A complaint handled well creates a more loyal customer than one who never had a problem:
1. Acknowledge and apologise immediately (even if you don't think it's your fault)
2. Fix it without hesitation — remake, refund, or both
3. Follow up if they're a regular

### Feedback Systems

- Google reviews: respond to every review, positive and negative
- Direct feedback: ask regulars directly what they think
- Staff feedback: front-line staff hear complaints before management does

### Net Promoter Score (NPS)

A simple 0–10 question: 'How likely are you to recommend us?' Promoters (9–10) are your most valuable marketing asset.
key_points: Regulars visit more and refer others — invest in them specifically
A well-handled complaint creates stronger loyalty than no complaint
Google review response signals professionalism to prospective customers
Front-line staff hear feedback first — create a channel to capture it

lessons.title: Professional Presentation
lessons.content:
## Professional Presentation

Your appearance and attitude set the tone for every shift. In a café, first impressions matter.
key_points: Neat uniform and personal hygiene are non-negotiable
Arrive 10 minutes before your shift to set up
Phone use on the floor is unprofessional

lessons.title: Communication & Teamwork
lessons.content:
## Communication & Teamwork

Café service is a team sport. Clear, calm communication keeps the bar running smoothly under pressure.
key_points: Call out orders clearly so the whole team hears
Ask for help before you fall behind — not after
Positive language keeps morale high during rushes

lessons.title: Understanding Your Role
lessons.content:
## Understanding Your Role

Every position on the café floor has a clear purpose. Knowing your role — and respecting others' — makes the whole team more effective.
key_points: Know your station and its responsibilities
Don't cut across other staff during service
Ask questions during downtime, not mid-rush

lessons.title: Espresso Drinks Explained
lessons.content:
## Espresso Drinks Explained

Knowing every drink on the menu — ingredients, ratios, and presentation — lets you serve confidently and answer customer questions.
key_points: Flat white: double ristretto + 150ml microfoam
Cappuccino: equal espresso, steamed milk, and foam
Long black: hot water first, then espresso poured over

lessons.title: Dietary & Allergy Awareness
lessons.content:
## Dietary & Allergy Awareness

Allergen awareness is a safety issue. Knowing common dietary requirements protects your customers.
key_points: Always clarify dairy-free requests — oat, almond, soy, coconut
Nut allergies can be severe — know your syrups and toppings
Coeliac = gluten-free; don't cross-contaminate

lessons.title: Upselling Naturally
lessons.content:
## Upselling Naturally

Good upselling feels like helpful service — not a sales pitch. It increases the average spend while making the customer feel looked after.
key_points: Suggest food pairings that actually complement the drink
Mention seasonal specials with genuine enthusiasm
Never pressure — offer once, then respect the answer

lessons.title: Greeting & Serving Customers
lessons.content:
## Greeting & Serving Customers

Every customer deserves to feel acknowledged and valued from the moment they walk in.
key_points: Make eye contact and greet within 30 seconds of arrival
Smile — even when you're busy, it reassures customers
Repeat orders back to confirm accuracy before making them

lessons.title: Handling Complaints
lessons.content:
## Handling Complaints

A complaint handled well creates a more loyal customer than one who never complained. Stay calm, listen, and act.
key_points: Never argue — acknowledge and apologise first
Fix it immediately: remake, refund, or both
Escalate to a manager if the customer remains unhappy

lessons.title: Pacing & Queue Management
lessons.content:
## Pacing & Queue Management

Managing a queue calmly — even when it's long — is a skill that keeps customers from walking out.
key_points: Acknowledge customers waiting — a nod goes a long way
Call out wait times honestly if there's a delay
Keep moving; visible hustle reassures customers drinks are coming

lessons.title: Hygiene Standards
lessons.content:
## Hygiene Standards

Food safety isn't optional — it protects your customers and your job. Personal hygiene is the foundation.
key_points: Wash hands for 20 seconds after touching anything non-food
Hair must be tied back or covered
Never handle food with broken skin or illness symptoms

lessons.title: Cleaning Protocols
lessons.content:
## Cleaning Protocols

A clean café is a safe café. Regular cleaning prevents contamination and keeps equipment performing.
key_points: Backflush the espresso machine every 30 minutes during service
Wipe steam wands immediately after every use
Sanitise surfaces between food preparation tasks

lessons.title: Temperature & Storage
lessons.content:
## Temperature & Storage

Food stored at the wrong temperature is a health risk. Know the danger zone and how to avoid it.
key_points: Danger zone: 5°C–60°C — bacteria multiply rapidly
Cold food must stay below 5°C; hot food above 60°C
FIFO: first in, first out for all perishables

lessons.title: Opening Procedures
lessons.content:
## Opening Procedures

A strong open sets the team up for a smooth service. Every step has a purpose.
key_points: Flush group heads and run blank shots to heat the machine
Check milk stock, cup stock, and syrup levels before service
Calibrate grinder with a test shot before opening

lessons.title: Station Workflow
lessons.content:
## Station Workflow

An efficient station layout reduces movement and increases speed. Everything should be within arm's reach.
key_points: Group head → tamper → knock box form the core triangle
Milk fridge below or beside the steam arm
Cups staged in order of size, handles facing out

lessons.title: Close-Down Procedures
lessons.content:
## Close-Down Procedures

A thorough close-down protects the equipment and sets the next shift up for success.
key_points: Backflush and clean group heads with detergent at end of day
Clean steam wands, drip tray, and grinder
Label and date all milk and prep items before refrigerating

lessons.title: Choosing Your Equipment
lessons.content:
## Choosing Your Equipment

The right home setup depends on your budget, space, and coffee goals. Getting this right from the start saves frustration later.
key_points: Entry: Breville Bambino / DeLonghi Dedica — affordable, capable
Mid: Breville Barista Express has a built-in grinder
Grinder matters more than the machine — invest there first

lessons.title: Your First Machine Setup
lessons.content:
## Your First Machine Setup

Setting up your machine correctly the first time prevents bad habits and inconsistent results.
key_points: Flush the group head before your first shot
Run hot water through the steam arm to purge it
Set water hardness to match your local supply

lessons.title: Basic Machine Maintenance
lessons.content:
## Basic Machine Maintenance

A well-maintained machine produces better coffee and lasts longer. Maintenance takes 5 minutes a day.
key_points: Rinse portafilter and baskets after every use
Backflush weekly with a blind filter (no detergent for non-commercial)
Descale every 2–3 months depending on water hardness

lessons.title: Grind Size & Espresso
lessons.content:
## Grind Size & Espresso

Grind size is the most important variable in home espresso. Small changes have a big impact on extraction.
key_points: Too fine = slow, bitter, over-extracted shot
Too coarse = fast, sour, under-extracted shot
Target: 25–30ml in 25–30 seconds for a double

lessons.title: Dose & Distribution
lessons.content:
## Dose & Distribution

How much coffee you use and how you distribute it in the basket directly affects extraction consistency.
key_points: Dose by weight: 18g for a double basket
Level the bed with a finger or distributor tool before tamping
Consistent distribution = even extraction and no channelling

lessons.title: Tamping at Home
lessons.content:
## Tamping at Home

Tamping seals the coffee bed so water flows through evenly rather than finding shortcuts (channelling).
key_points: Tamp level — a tilted tamp causes uneven extraction
Apply 15–20kg of pressure, then release cleanly
Polish the puck with a slight twist — optional but satisfying

lessons.title: Steaming Milk at Home
lessons.content:
## Steaming Milk at Home

Home steam wands are smaller than commercial ones but the technique is the same. Cold milk and patience are your best tools.
key_points: Start with cold milk — it gives you more time to texture
Submerge tip just below the surface to stretch (add air)
Then plunge deeper to spin and heat to 65°C

lessons.title: Milk Temperature
lessons.content:
## Milk Temperature

Temperature affects taste and texture. Too hot and the milk tastes scalded; too cool and it's thin and flat.
key_points: Target: 60–65°C (just uncomfortable to hold)
A thermometer is worth it when learning — saves a lot of waste
Whole milk gives the best texture; oat milk is next best

lessons.title: Basic Latte Art at Home
lessons.content:
## Basic Latte Art at Home

You don't need a commercial machine to pour a heart. The fundamentals are the same — it just takes practice.
key_points: Swirl your milk jug to knock out large bubbles before pouring
Tilt the cup, pour into the centre, then push through at the end
Start with a heart — it's the foundation of all latte art

lessons.title: Flat White & Latte at Home
lessons.content:
## Flat White & Latte at Home

The flat white and latte differ mainly in ratio. Both require well-textured microfoam.
key_points: Flat white: 30ml double ristretto + 100–120ml milk
Latte: 30ml espresso + 180–220ml milk
Both need glossy, velvety microfoam — no big bubbles

lessons.title: Cold Brew at Home
lessons.content:
## Cold Brew at Home

Cold brew is one of the easiest methods — and the most forgiving. No heat, no rush.
key_points: Coarse grind, 1:8 ratio coffee to cold water
Steep 12–18 hours in the fridge
Strain through a paper filter to remove fine sediment

lessons.title: Filter Coffee Methods
lessons.content:
## Filter Coffee Methods

Pour-over and AeroPress are simple, affordable, and produce outstanding coffee at home.
key_points: V60: 15g coffee, 250ml at 93°C, 3-minute brew
AeroPress: more forgiving — 15g, 200ml, 2-minute brew
Use a gooseneck kettle for pour-over — control matters

lessons.title: Tasting Your Espresso
lessons.content:
## Tasting Your Espresso

Learning to taste your shot diagnostically is the key skill for dialling in at home.
key_points: Sour/sharp = under-extracted → grind finer or increase dose
Bitter/harsh = over-extracted → grind coarser or reduce dose
Balanced, sweet, complex = you're dialled in

lessons.title: Adjusting Your Grinder
lessons.content:
## Adjusting Your Grinder

Small grinder adjustments have a big impact. Change one step at a time and taste the result.
key_points: Make one adjustment at a time — never two at once
The shot time is your feedback: faster = too coarse, slower = too fine
Write down your settings so you can replicate them

lessons.title: Keeping Records
lessons.content:
## Keeping Records

Home baristas who keep notes improve faster. Even a simple notes app works.
key_points: Record: grinder setting, dose, yield, time, tasting notes
Reference the same coffee bag to understand its range
When you nail it — write everything down before you forget

lessons.title: What 'Dialing In' Means
lessons.content:
## What 'Dialing In' Means

Dialing in means adjusting the grinder, dose, yield, and recipe until the espresso tastes balanced, sweet, clean, and repeatable.

### Standard Starting Recipe

| Variable | Target |
|---|---|
| Dose | 20g |
| Yield | 40g |
| Ratio | 1:2 |
| Time | 25–32 seconds |
| Temperature | 92–94°C |
| Pressure | 8–9 bar |

This is only a starting point. Taste is always the final judge.

---

### The Main Rule

If the shot runs too fast → Grind finer

If the shot runs too slow → Grind coarser

### Fast shots often taste:
- Sour
- Thin
- Sharp
- Salty
- Weak

### Slow shots often taste:
- Bitter
- Dry
- Harsh
- Hollow
- Burnt

Time tells you where to look. Taste tells you what to do.
key_points: Dialing in = adjusting grind, dose, yield until balanced
Standard start: 20g in / 40g out / 25–32s / 92–94°C
Fast shot = grind finer; Slow shot = grind coarser
Taste is always the final judge — not numbers

quiz.question: A shot runs in 18 seconds and tastes sour and thin. What should you do?
quiz.explanation: A fast shot (under 25s) with sour/thin flavour indicates under-extraction. Grinding finer increases resistance, slows the shot, and improves extraction.

lessons.title: The Dial-In Workflow
lessons.content:
## The Dial-In Workflow

A repeatable workflow removes guesswork and gets you to a great shot faster.

---

## Step 1 — Set Your Recipe

Choose:
- Coffee dose
- Yield
- Shot time
- Brew temperature
- Flavour goal

Example: 20g in / 40g out / 28 seconds / 93°C

---

## Step 2 — Purge the Grinder

After every grind adjustment:
