→ Purge 3–6g of coffee.

Commercial grinders retain old coffee grounds inside the chamber. The first shot after adjustment may still contain the previous setting — purging flushes it out.

---

## Step 3 — Weigh Everything

Weigh:
- Dry coffee dose (in)
- Liquid espresso yield (out)
- Shot time

Do not guess. Scales are non-negotiable.

---

## Step 4 — Taste and Record

Use a dial-in log to track every shot:

| Time | Dose | Yield | Time | Taste | Adjustment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8:00am | 20g | 40g | 22s | Sour/thin | Finer |
| 8:10am | 20g | 40g | 29s | Sweet/balanced | Keep |
| 11:30am | 20g | 40g | 24s | Sharp | Finer slightly |

---

### The Golden Rule

Change one variable at a time. If you adjust grind and dose simultaneously, you cannot know which change fixed the problem.
key_points: Always purge 3–6g after every grind adjustment
Weigh dose in AND yield out — never guess
Record every shot: dose, yield, time, taste, adjustment
Change only ONE variable per shot

lessons.title: Understanding Grind Direction
lessons.content:
## Understanding Grind Direction

### Finer Grind

A finer grind:
- Slows the shot
- Increases resistance
- Increases extraction
- Increases sweetness and body
- Can create bitterness if overdone

Use finer when:
- Espresso runs fast
- Espresso tastes sour
- Espresso is watery
- Crema disappears quickly
- Blonding occurs early

---

### Coarser Grind

A coarser grind:
- Speeds up the shot
- Reduces resistance
- Lowers extraction
- Creates cleaner flavour
- Can taste weak if too coarse

Use coarser when:
- Espresso runs slow
- Espresso tastes bitter
- Espresso tastes dry
- Machine struggles to push water through puck
- Shot drips instead of flowing

---

### Grind Size Summary

| Direction | Effect | When to Use |
|---|---|---|
| Finer | Slower, more extraction | Sour, fast, watery |
| Coarser | Faster, less extraction | Bitter, slow, dripping |
key_points: Finer = slower shot, more extraction, more body
Coarser = faster shot, less extraction, cleaner
Go finer for sour/fast shots, coarser for bitter/slow shots
Early blonding = grind finer

quiz.question: Your espresso shot is running in 38 seconds and tastes bitter and dry. What adjustment do you make?
options: Add more coffee to the basket
quiz.explanation: A slow shot (38s) with bitter, dry flavour indicates over-extraction. Grinding coarser opens up the grind, speeds the flow, and reduces extraction.

lessons.title: Flavour Extraction — Under & Over
lessons.content:
## Flavour Extraction — Under & Over

### Under-Extraction

Under-extracted espresso tastes:
- Sour
- Salty
- Sharp
- Thin
- Watery
- Grassy

Common causes:
- Grind too coarse
- Shot too fast
- Yield too low
- Water too cool
- Poor puck prep
- Channeling

Fixes:
- Grind finer
- Increase yield
- Increase brew temperature
- Improve puck prep and distribution

---

### Over-Extraction

Over-extracted espresso tastes:
- Bitter
- Dry
- Harsh
- Burnt
- Woody
- Hollow

Common causes:
- Grind too fine
- Shot too slow
- Yield too high
- Water too hot
- Dirty grinder
- Old coffee oils

Fixes:
- Grind coarser
- Reduce yield
- Lower temperature
- Clean grinder
- Check roast freshness

---

### Quick Reference

| Flavour | Extraction State | Primary Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Sour/thin | Under | Grind finer |
| Bitter/dry | Over | Grind coarser |
| Sour + bitter | Channeling | Better puck prep |
| Flat/dull | Old beans/burr wear | Fresh beans or new burrs |
key_points: Under-extracted = sour, salty, thin, grassy
Over-extracted = bitter, dry, harsh, hollow
Sour + bitter together usually means channeling
Clean grinder and fresh beans prevent over-extraction drift

quiz.question: Your espresso tastes sour AND bitter at the same time. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.explanation: Sour and bitter simultaneously is the classic signature of channeling — water finds a fast path through part of the puck (sour) while over-extracting in another (bitter). Fix with better distribution and puck prep.

lessons.title: Roast Profile Dialing
lessons.content:
## Roast Profile Dialing

Different roast levels require different approaches. Understanding each profile lets you dial in faster and with more accuracy.

---

## Light Roast Espresso

Light roast coffee is denser and harder to extract.

Typical issues: Sourness, thin body, sharp acidity, fast blonding

Recommended approach:
- Grind finer
- Higher temperature (94–96°C)
- Longer ratio
- Longer extraction

Target recipe: 20g in / 48g out / 32–36s / 94–96°C

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| Sour but clean | Increase yield |
| Sour and fast | Grind finer |
| Bitter and sharp | Lower temperature |
| Dry and hollow | Coarser or shorter yield |

---

## Medium Roast Espresso

Most balanced and forgiving roast profile.

Target recipe: 20g in / 40g out / 28–30s / 92–94°C

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| Sour | Grind finer |
| Bitter | Grind coarser |
| Weak | Reduce yield |
| Heavy/muddy | Grind coarser |

---

## Dark Roast Espresso

Dark roast is highly soluble — it extracts easily and quickly.

Typical issues: Bitterness, dryness, smokiness, ashy flavours

Recommended approach:
- Grind slightly coarser
- Lower temperature (90–92°C)
- Shorter yield

Target recipe: 20g in / 34–38g out / 24–28s / 90–92°C

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| Bitter/dry | Coarser + lower temperature |
| Burnt | Clean machine + lower temperature |
| Muddy | Grind coarser |
key_points: Light roast: finer grind, higher temp (94–96°C), longer ratio
Medium roast: 20g/40g/28–30s/92–94°C — most forgiving
Dark roast: slightly coarser, lower temp (90–92°C), shorter yield
Light roasts extract harder — sour is the most common problem

quiz.question: You're dialing in a light roast espresso at 92°C and it tastes sour and sharp. What is the best adjustment?
options: Grind finer and raise temperature to 95°C
quiz.explanation: Light roasts are dense and hard to extract. Grinding finer increases extraction, and raising temperature to 94–96°C gives the water more energy to extract from these denser beans.

lessons.title: Temperature & Grinder Heat
lessons.content:
## Temperature & Grinder Heat

Commercial grinders heat up significantly during service — and this changes extraction.

### As Burrs Warm:
- Coffee becomes more brittle
- Shots may run faster
- Espresso may lose body
- Static may change
- Dose consistency may drift

---

## During Rush Periods

Check espresso every 15–20 minutes.

- If shots speed up → Adjust finer slightly
- If shots slow after rush → Adjust coarser slightly

Avoid large changes. Small, incremental adjustments maintain consistency.

---

## Opening Warm-Up Routine

1. Turn grinder on
2. Run small amount of coffee through (purge stale grounds)
3. Pull 2–3 test shots
4. Allow grinder and machine to fully stabilise
5. Begin dial-in

Never start service on the first shot of the day without testing first.

---

## Key Insight

Grinder heat is one of the most overlooked causes of shot drift during service. A shot that was perfect at 8am may run 4–5 seconds faster by 10am if no adjustment is made.
key_points: Grinders heat up during service, making shots run faster
Check espresso every 15–20 minutes during busy periods
Go finer slightly as the rush builds
Always warm up and pull test shots before service begins

lessons.title: Humidity, Weather & Environmental Effects
lessons.content:
## Humidity, Weather & Environmental Effects

Coffee is hygroscopic — it absorbs moisture from the air. Environmental changes can dramatically affect your espresso without you touching a single setting.

---

## High Humidity Conditions

Common in: Sydney, Brisbane, Gold Coast, Cairns, Darwin

Effects:
- More clumping in the chute
- Slower shots
- Heavier body
- Dull or muted flavour
- Chute blockages

Adjustments:
- Go slightly coarser
- Clean chute more frequently
- Keep hopper covered when not in use

---

## Dry Conditions

Common in: Canberra, inland NSW, winter mornings, air-conditioned cafés

Effects:
- Static buildup
- Faster shots
- Coffee spraying from chute
- Lighter body

Adjustments:
- Go slightly finer
- Improve distribution technique
- Check dose weight carefully

---

## Temperature Swings — Cold Morning to Hot Lunch

| Time | Condition | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Opening | Cold machine/grinder | Shots slower |
| Mid-morning | Warming up | Shots stabilising |
| Lunch rush | Hot grinder | Shots faster |

Best practice — re-check espresso at:
- Open
- Mid-morning
- After each rush
- After opening a new bag of coffee
key_points: High humidity = shots slow down, go slightly coarser
Dry air = static, faster shots, go slightly finer
Cold morning → hot rush means shots will speed up during service
Re-check espresso at open, mid-morning, after rushes, and with new bags

quiz.question: You work in Brisbane. After a humid night you open the café and the shots are running slow and clumping. What do you do?
options: Grind slightly coarser and clean the chute
quiz.explanation: High humidity causes coffee to absorb moisture, making it grind slightly finer than normal and slowing shots. Going slightly coarser and cleaning the chute to remove clumps will restore balance.

lessons.title: Mahlkönig EK43 / EK43S
lessons.content:
## Mahlkönig EK43 / EK43S

### Overview

Common uses: Espresso, filter coffee, batch brew, specialty cafés, roasteries

Known for: High clarity, sweetness, and flavour separation

---

## Adjustment

The EK43 uses a front hand wheel adjustment.

- Lower numbers → Finer
- Higher numbers → Coarser

Always purge after adjustment. Make very small movements for espresso — the EK43 is extremely sensitive.

---

## EK43 Characteristics

Produces:
- High clarity
- Clean flavour separation
- Bright acidity
- Lower body than SP2-style grinders

The EK43 is often described as a 'clarity machine' — it reveals the true character of the coffee with less body than traditional espresso grinders.

---

## Cleaning Schedule

Daily:
- Brush intake and chute
- Purge stale coffee
- Wipe exterior

Weekly:
- Brush burr chamber thoroughly
- Inspect burrs for wear
- Vacuum loose grinds from chamber

---

## EK43 Troubleshooting

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Fast shots | Finer |
| Muddy espresso | Coarser |
| Sour espresso | Finer or longer yield |
| Bitter espresso | Coarser or shorter yield |
key_points: EK43 uses front wheel — lower numbers = finer
Known for high clarity, separation, and bright acidity
Make tiny adjustments — extremely sensitive for espresso
Daily brushing of intake and chute is essential

quiz.question: On the Mahlkönig EK43, you need to grind finer for espresso. Which direction do you turn the hand wheel?
options: It has no hand wheel — use the top dial
quiz.explanation: On the EK43, lower numbers on the front hand wheel produce a finer grind. Always purge 3–5g after any adjustment before pulling the next shot.

lessons.title: Mahlkönig E65S / E80S / GBW
lessons.content:
## Mahlkönig E65S / E80S / GBW

### Overview

Modern specialty café grinders designed for high-volume, precise workflow.

Known for:
- Grind-by-weight (GBW) accuracy
- Fast workflow
- High consistency
- Low waste

---

## Adjustment

Uses a micrometric adjustment dial.

Rules:
- Small movements only
- Purge after every adjustment
- Verify weight after every grind change

---

## The Critical GBW Lesson

Even with an accurate dose weight, extraction can still drift due to:
- Humidity
- Grinder heat
- Coffee age and degassing
- Bean density
- Roast development

Taste is still the final judge — not the scale.

The GBW function ensures a consistent dose, but it does not replace the need to taste your espresso regularly.

---

## Cleaning Schedule

Daily:
- Clean chute
- Purge stale coffee
- Wipe scale sensor area (keep clean for accuracy)

Weekly:
- Brush burr chamber
- Clean scale sensors with dry cloth
- Inspect retention areas for buildup

---

## Important Note

Changing grind size changes the dose output on timed grinders. After any grind adjustment on a GBW model, always re-verify dose weight before service.
key_points: E65S/GBW uses micrometric dial — small movements only
GBW dose accuracy does not replace taste-testing
Grind changes affect dose weight — always re-verify
Clean scale sensors daily for accurate dose readings

lessons.title: Anfim SP II
lessons.content:
## Anfim SP II

### Overview

One of the most respected espresso grinders in Australia, found in specialty and high-volume cafés everywhere.

Known for:
- Large flat burrs
- Heavy body espresso
- Sweet extraction
- Excellent milk coffee texture
- Stable café performance

Popular in: Specialty cafés, high-volume venues, milk-heavy menus

---

## SP2 Flavour Profile

Produces:
- Strong sweetness
- Heavy body
- Thick crema
- Rounded acidity

Compared to EK43:
- EK43 → Clarity and separation
- SP2 → Sweetness and body

---

## Adjustment

The SP2 uses a collar adjustment.

⚠️ Make VERY small movements. Large flat-burr grinders react strongly to adjustment changes — even a tiny movement has a significant effect on shot time.

---

## SP2 During Rushes

As the grinder heats during service:
- Shots may speed up
- Espresso loses body
- Extraction decreases

→ Adjust slightly finer as the rush builds to maintain consistency.

---

## Cleaning Schedule

Daily: Empty hopper, brush chute, purge stale coffee, wipe exterior

Weekly: Brush burr chamber, clean declumper, inspect burrs for wear

---

## SP2 Troubleshooting

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Espresso suddenly fast | Grinder heat → finer slightly |
| Flat/dull flavour | Burr wear — inspect and replace |
| Clumping | Clean declumper |
| Muddy espresso | Grind coarser |
key_points: SP2 uses collar adjustment — very small movements only
Known for heavy sweetness, thick body, and crema
Go finer during rushes as grinder heats up
Flat/dull flavour during service often means worn burrs

quiz.question: You've just made a grind adjustment on the Anfim SP II. What is the most important next step before pulling a shot?
options: Pull the shot immediately to test
Purge 3–6g of coffee through the grinder first
Turn the grinder off and back on
quiz.explanation: After any grind adjustment on any commercial grinder, you must purge 3–6g to flush retained coffee from the chamber. The first grounds out will still be from the old setting.

lessons.title: Victoria Arduino Mythos
lessons.content:
## Victoria Arduino Mythos

### Overview

Extremely common in Australian specialty cafés.

Popular models: Mythos One, Mythos Two, MY75, MYG75

Known for:
- Temperature-controlled burr chamber (Clima Pro technology)
- High consistency throughout service
- Stable extraction during rush periods
- Fast, clean workflow

---

## Mythos Characteristics

Produces:
- Balanced sweetness
- Smooth, textured body
- Consistent extraction

Compared to EK43:
- EK43 → Clarity
- Mythos → Balance and texture

---

## Adjustment

The Mythos uses micrometric adjustment.

Rules:
- Tiny changes only
- Purge after every change
- Re-weigh dose after grind adjustment

---

## Timed Dose Programming

1. Enter programming mode
2. Select dose button
3. Adjust grind time
4. Weigh the resulting dose
5. Fine-tune and save

⚠️ Important: Changing grind size changes dose weight. Always re-weigh after any grind adjustment and re-program if needed.

---

## Cleaning Schedule

Daily: Brush chute, wipe portafilter fork, remove coffee oils from fork area

Weekly: Brush burr chamber, clean declumper, vacuum loose coffee from chamber

---

## Mythos Troubleshooting

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Dose drifting | Reprogram timer |
| Clumping | Clean declumper |
| Fast shots during rush | Grind finer slightly |
| Bitter espresso | Grind coarser |
key_points: Mythos has temperature-controlled burrs — more stable than most grinders during rushes
Uses micrometric adjustment — tiny changes only
Changing grind size changes timed dose — always re-weigh and reprogram
Weekly declumper cleaning prevents clumping issues

lessons.title: Mazzer Super Jolly, Major & Robur
lessons.content:
## Mazzer Super Jolly, Major & Robur

### Overview

Traditional Italian café workhorses — extremely common in Australian cafés.

Known for:
- Reliability and durability
- High volume output
- Thick, heavy body espresso
- Strong milk coffee performance

---

## Adjustment

All Mazzer models use collar adjustment.

⚠️ Important: When moving to a finer setting, run the grinder while adjusting to avoid jamming the burrs. Never force the collar on a static grinder.

---

## Timed Dose Programming

1. Adjust the grind to your target setting
2. Grind a test dose
3. Weigh the dose on your scale
4. Adjust the timer up or down
5. Save and repeat until dose is consistent

---

## Cleaning Schedule

Daily: Brush chute, empty hopper at end of day, remove stale coffee from chamber

Weekly: Brush burr chamber thoroughly, vacuum grinds from all internal areas, remove oily residue from chute

---

## Mazzer Troubleshooting

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Slow shots | Grind coarser |
| Fast shots | Grind finer |
| Rancid/off flavour | Deep clean — old oil buildup |
| Inconsistent dose | Recalibrate timer |

---

## Key Note on Collar Adjustment

Moving finer on a Mazzer without running the grinder risks burr contact. This is the #1 maintenance mistake on these machines. Always run the grinder while moving finer.
key_points: Mazzer uses collar adjustment — always run grinder when moving finer
Known for heavy body and durability — suits milk-heavy menus
Rancid flavour = deep clean needed for oil buildup
Inconsistent dose = timer recalibration required

quiz.question: You need to adjust the Mazzer Super Jolly to a finer grind. What is the correct procedure?
options: Turn the collar finer while the grinder is off
Run the grinder while slowly moving the collar finer
Remove the hopper and adjust from inside
Use the timed dose button to compensate
quiz.explanation: On Mazzer grinders, always run the grinder while adjusting to a finer setting. Moving the collar finer on a static (non-running) grinder can cause the burrs to jam or grind against each other.

lessons.title: La Marzocco Swan
lessons.content:
## La Marzocco Swan

### Overview

Modern premium espresso grinder designed to match La Marzocco's top-tier machines.

Designed for:
- Precision workflow
- Low retention
- Grind-by-weight accuracy
- Specialty cafés

---

## Swan Characteristics

Produces:
- High clarity
- Sweetness
- Consistent extraction
- Low retention workflow (less stale coffee between shots)

---

## Adjustment

The Swan uses micrometric adjustment.

Rules:
- Small changes only
- Purge after every adjustment
- Verify dose weight after grind changes
- Pull multiple test shots before committing

---

## Cleaning Schedule

Daily:
- Empty hopper at close
- Brush chute
- Purge stale coffee at open
- Wipe exterior

Weekly:
- Clean burr chamber
- Inspect and clean scale sensors
- Clean retention areas

---

## Swan Troubleshooting

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| Weight accurate but shot fast | Grind finer |
| Dose inconsistent | Clean scale sensors |
| Thin espresso | Finer or longer yield |
| Dry espresso | Grind coarser |

---

## Important Note

The Swan is a low-retention grinder — there is very little coffee sitting inside the chamber between shots. This means adjustments take effect almost immediately. You may only need a 1–2g purge compared to 5–6g on older grinders.
key_points: Swan is low-retention — adjustments take effect immediately
Uses micrometric adjustment — small movements only
Clean scale sensors weekly for consistent dose accuracy
Low retention means less purge needed than traditional grinders

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Chart
lessons.content:
## Troubleshooting Chart

Use this chart to quickly diagnose and fix common espresso and grinder problems during service.

| Problem | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Shot runs 18–22 sec | Grind too coarse | Grind finer |
| Shot runs 35–45 sec | Grind too fine | Grind coarser |
| Sour/thin espresso | Under-extracted | Grind finer |
| Bitter/dry espresso | Over-extracted | Grind coarser |
| Sour + bitter together | Channeling | Better puck prep and distribution |
| Clumping in chute | Dirty chute or humidity | Clean grinder, go slightly coarser |
| Static spray | Dry air | Better distribution, check dose |
| Flat, dull flavour | Old beans or worn burrs | Fresh beans or inspect burrs |
| Dose drifting (timed grinders) | Timer needs recalibration | Reprogram timer |
| Shots speed up during rush | Grinder heat | Adjust finer slightly |

---

## Quick Decision Framework

Step 1: Check the time
- Fast (< 25s) → go finer
- Slow (> 32s) → go coarser

Step 2: Taste
- Sour → finer
- Bitter → coarser
- Both → puck prep

Step 3: Look for other causes
- Dose drifting → timer
- Clumping → clean chute
- Flat flavour → fresh beans or burr check
key_points: Fast shot + sour = under-extracted, grind finer
Slow shot + bitter = over-extracted, grind coarser
Sour AND bitter = channeling, not a grind issue
Shots speeding up during service = grinder heat, go finer

quiz.question: During a busy Saturday service your shots were perfect at 8am. By 10am they're running 5 seconds faster. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: New bag of coffee — change recipe completely
Grinder heat causing shots to speed up — adjust finer slightly
Machine pressure has dropped — call a technician
quiz.explanation: Shot drift during service is most commonly caused by grinder heat. As the burrs warm up, coffee becomes more brittle and grinds finer, causing shots to run faster. The fix is a small finer adjustment to compensate.

lessons.title: Daily Barista Routine
lessons.content:
## Daily Barista Routine

A consistent daily routine is what separates good baristas from great ones. These habits protect your espresso quality through every stage of service.

---

## Opening Routine

1. Turn on machine and grinder
2. Check roast date on coffee bag
3. Empty old beans if needed (especially overnight)
4. Purge grinder to remove stale grounds
5. Pull 2–3 test shots
6. Dial in espresso
7. Record recipe

---

## During Service

Check every 30–60 minutes:
- Dose (still on weight?)
- Yield (still hitting target?)
- Time (still within range?)
- Flavour (taste a test shot)
- Weather changes (temperature, humidity)
- Grinder heat (shots speeding up?)

---

## Close Routine

1. Empty hopper of remaining beans
2. Brush all loose coffee from grinder
3. Purge any stale coffee from the chamber
4. Clean the chute
5. Wipe exterior of grinder
6. Report any issues to manager

---

## The Professionals' Mindset

> A perfect 28-second shot can still taste terrible.
> A 22-second shot can taste amazing if the recipe suits the coffee.

Dialing in is not chasing numbers. It is understanding your coffee and making it taste its best. Time is a guide. Taste is the destination.
key_points: Always purge before service and pull test shots at open
Check dose, yield, time, and flavour every 30–60 minutes during service
Empty hopper and clean chute at close every day
Time tells you where to look — taste tells you what to do

lessons.title: Assessment — Dialing In Mastery
lessons.content:
## Assessment — Dialing In Mastery

Test your knowledge with these five assessment questions from the Bean Culture grinder course.

---

### Q1: Fast and Sour

A shot runs 20 seconds and tastes sour. What should you do?

✅ Answer: Grind finer

---

### Q2: Why Purge?

Why must you purge after a grind adjustment?

✅ Answer: To remove retained coffee from the previous setting. Commercial grinders hold old grounds inside the chamber. Without purging, your next shot still contains the old grind.

---

### Q3: Humid Weather

What usually happens during humid weather?

✅ Answer: Shots slow down and clumping increases. Moisture causes coffee to grind slightly finer than normal. Adjust slightly coarser and clean the chute more frequently.

---

### Q4: Timed Grinder Rule

Why must timed grinders be re-weighed after grind changes?

✅ Answer: Grind size affects how fast the burrs move coffee through — a finer grind produces more grams per second. After any adjustment, the dose output changes and the timer must be recalibrated.

---

### Q5: Bitter and Dry

What causes bitter, dry espresso?

✅ Answer: Over-extraction — usually caused by grind too fine, shot too slow, or water too hot.

---

## Practical Assessment Scenario

You are given: 20g in / 40g out / 21 seconds / Sour and thin flavour

To pass, you must:
1. Identify the problem (under-extraction)
2. Make the correct adjustment (grind finer)
3. Purge the grinder correctly (3–6g)
4. Pull a new shot
5. Taste and evaluate the result
6. Explain why the change worked

Passing criteria:
- Uses scales correctly throughout
- Makes small, controlled adjustments
- Purges correctly after every change
- Maintains recipe consistency
- Diagnoses flavour accurately

---

> Time tells you where to look. Taste tells you what to do.
key_points: Fast + sour = under-extraction → grind finer
Always purge after grind adjustment to clear retained coffee
Humid weather slows shots and causes clumping
Timed grinders must be re-weighed and reprogrammed after grind changes

quiz.question: You are given 20g in / 40g out / 21 seconds / sour and thin. What is the correct diagnosis and first action?
options: Under-extraction — grind finer and purge before next shot
quiz.explanation: 21 seconds is too fast for a 20g/40g recipe (target 25–32s) and sour/thin flavour confirms under-extraction. Grind finer, purge 3–6g, then pull a new shot.

data.title: Coffee Foundations
data.objective: Teach trainers the origin story of coffee they can relay to any student.
data.content:
## Coffee Foundations

Coffee is a seed from the coffee cherry — a fruit that grows on trees at high altitude in the tropics.

### The Four Flavour Pillars
1. Farming — Altitude, soil, shade, and rainfall
2. Processing — How the cherry is removed from the bean
3. Roasting — Heat transformation that develops flavour
4. Brewing — Extraction of soluble flavour from the bean

### Arabica vs Robusta
- Arabica — 60–70% of world production. Higher altitude, more complex, lower caffeine, sweeter
- Robusta — More resilient, more bitter, higher caffeine, cheaper to produce

### Origin Affects Flavour
- Ethiopian coffee → floral, fruity, bright
- Brazilian coffee → nutty, chocolatey, low acidity
- Colombian coffee → balanced, caramel, red fruit
data.trainer_script: "Coffee starts as a cherry on a tree. Inside that cherry is the seed — which is the coffee bean. Everything that happens to that seed from the farm to your cup affects what it tastes like. So when someone says they don't like coffee, usually what they mean is they haven't found the right coffee yet."
key_points: Coffee = seed of the coffee cherry
4 pillars: farming, processing, roasting, brewing
Arabica = quality; Robusta = strength/body
Origin = flavour direction

student_questions.q: Why does my home coffee taste bad?
student_questions.a: Usually stale beans, wrong grind, or wrong recipe.

student_questions.q: Is dark roast stronger?
student_questions.a: Stronger in flavour, but actually less caffeine than light roast.

checklist: Show green beans if available
Show roasted beans side by side
Ask students what coffee they drink at home
Connect origin to flavour preference

data.title: Coffee Processing
data.objective: Explain the three main processing methods and how they affect cup flavour.
data.content:
## Coffee Processing

After the coffee cherry is harvested, the fruit must be removed from the bean. The method used dramatically changes the flavour.

### Washed Process
The cherry skin and pulp are removed immediately. Beans are fermented then dried.

Flavour: Clean, bright, higher acidity. The terroir shines through.

### Natural Process
The whole cherry is dried in the sun with the fruit still on the bean.

Flavour: Fruity, heavier body, sweeter perception, wine-like notes.

### Honey Process
The skin is removed but some mucilage (the sticky layer) remains during drying.

Flavour: Sweet balance between washed and natural.
data.trainer_script: "Think of it this way. Washed coffee is like clean apple juice — pure, transparent, bright. Natural coffee is like a fruit smoothie — heavy, fruity, complex. Honey is somewhere in between. When you taste a coffee and it's really fruity and jammy, it's almost certainly natural processed."
key_points: Washed = clean, bright, transparent
Natural = fruity, heavy, wine-like
Honey = sweet balance
Processing is one of the biggest flavour factors

student_questions.q: Which one tastes better?
student_questions.a: Depends on preference. Washed suits people who like clean bright coffee. Natural suits fruity and sweet preference.

student_questions.q: Does it affect caffeine?
student_questions.a: Not significantly. Caffeine is in the bean itself.

checklist: Use the apple juice vs smoothie analogy
If possible, taste a washed and natural side by side
Ask students to describe the difference before explaining

data.title: Roasting Overview
data.objective: Teach trainers to explain the roasting process and how it creates flavour.
data.content:
## Roasting Overview

Roasting transforms green coffee beans into the aromatic brown beans we brew. Heat removes moisture and develops complex sugars and flavour compounds.

### Light Roast
- Dropped before second crack (~196–205°C)
- More origin character preserved
- Fruity, floral, bright acidity
- Higher caffeine

### Medium Roast
- Balanced roast character and origin
- Caramel, chocolate, nutty notes
- Most popular commercial roast

### Dark Roast
- Into or beyond second crack (218°C+)
- Roast character dominates
- Smoky, bitter, full-bodied
- Lower origin character

### Giesen Roaster
Bean Culture uses the Giesen roaster — a professional drum roaster that gives precise control over temperature curves. Roasts are profiled to match each bean's ideal development.
data.trainer_script: "Roasting is where the magic happens. A green coffee bean has almost no aroma. Put it in a roaster at 200 degrees for 10 minutes and suddenly it smells incredible. The heat breaks down the cell structure and creates hundreds of flavour compounds. Our roaster here — the Giesen — is one of the best in the world for controlling that process."
key_points: Roasting = moisture removal + flavour development
Light = more origin, higher caffeine
Dark = more roast character, less origin
Giesen = precision drum roaster

student_questions.q: Is dark roast more caffeine?
student_questions.a: No — dark roast actually has slightly less caffeine. The bean loses mass during roasting.

student_questions.q: How long does roasting take?
student_questions.a: Typically 10–15 minutes depending on the profile.

checklist: Point out the Giesen roaster during roastery tour
Show green vs roasted beans
Smell both so students can feel the difference
Explain light/medium/dark in simple terms

data.title: Espresso Extraction
data.objective: Teach the Bean Culture espresso recipe and the science of extraction.
data.content:
## Espresso Extraction

### Bean Culture Recipe
- Dose: 20g coffee in
- Yield: 40g espresso out
- Time: 25–27 seconds

### The Extraction Stages
Extraction happens in a specific order:
1. Acids — First to extract. Give brightness and fruit.
2. Sugars — Next. Give sweetness and body.
3. Bitters — Last. Give depth but also harshness if over-extracted.

### What Balanced Espresso Feels Like
- Sweet
- Smooth
- Rounded
- Long finish
- No harsh aftertaste

Pressure is 9 bar. Water temperature is 93–95°C. These are fixed. The only variable the barista controls is grind size.
data.trainer_script: "Our recipe is simple to remember: 20 in, 40 out, 25–27 seconds. That's the target every time. A great espresso is sweet, smooth, and leaves a clean long finish — not a bitter coating on your tongue. If it's harsh at the end, something's off."
key_points: 20g in / 40g out / 25–27 seconds
Extraction order: acids → sugars → bitters
Balanced = sweet, smooth, rounded, long finish
Grind size is the primary variable

student_questions.q: Why 20g specifically?
student_questions.a: It's calibrated to the basket size and machine pressure to extract optimally.

student_questions.q: What if my shot tastes bitter?
student_questions.a: Usually over-extracted — go coarser on the grind.

checklist: Demonstrate the recipe step by step
Let students taste the espresso
Ask them to describe the finish
Connect taste to extraction stage

data.title: Under / Over / Balanced Extraction
data.objective: Train the palate to identify and fix extraction problems.
data.content:
## Extraction Diagnosis

### Under Extracted
- Taste: Sour, thin, hollow, sharp
- Cause: Too coarse, too short, too little dose
- Fix: Grind finer to slow the shot

### Over Extracted
- Taste: Bitter, harsh, dry, coating
- Cause: Too fine, too long, too hot
- Fix: Grind coarser to speed the shot

### Balanced
- Taste: Sweet, smooth, rounded, clean long finish
- Target: Always

### Trainer Tasting Drill
Prepare three shots deliberately:
1. Under extracted (coarse grind, fast shot)
2. Over extracted (fine grind, long shot)
3. Balanced (correct recipe)

Ask students to taste all three without telling them which is which.
data.trainer_script: "We're chasing balance, not strength. Strength is how concentrated it is — that's determined by dose and yield. Balance is about flavour — that's determined by time and grind. A perfect espresso isn't the strongest one. It's the one that tastes exactly right."
key_points: Under = sour, thin, hollow, fast shot
Over = bitter, harsh, dry, slow shot
Balanced = sweet, smooth, rounded
We chase balance, not strength

student_questions.q: My coffee tastes sour, is it the beans?
student_questions.a: Usually under-extraction. Try grinding finer before changing beans.

student_questions.q: How do I know it's balanced?
student_questions.a: It should be sweet and smooth with no harsh aftertaste.

checklist: Pull one under-extracted shot deliberately
Pull one over-extracted shot deliberately
Pull a balanced shot
Let students taste all three blind
Ask them to describe each before revealing which is which

data.title: Grinder Control
data.objective: Teach trainers to explain grinder adjustments clearly to students.
data.content:
## Grinder Control

The grinder is the most important variable in espresso. Think of it as a time machine — adjusting it changes how long water takes to pass through the coffee.

### The Grinder = Time Machine
- Finer grind → more surface area → more resistance → water takes longer → slower shot
- Coarser grind → less surface area → less resistance → water passes faster → faster shot

### Adjustment Rules
1. Change one thing at a time. Don't adjust dose AND grind at the same time.
2. Small adjustments have big effects. One click can change 3–5 seconds.
3. Always purge the grinder after any adjustment — the channel still holds old grounds.

### When to Adjust
- Shot runs under 25 seconds → go finer
- Shot runs over 27 seconds → go coarser
data.trainer_script: "The grinder is your time machine. Finer settings slow time down — the water takes longer to get through. Coarser settings speed time up. When I say adjust the grind, I mean change the speed the shot is running. The recipe stays the same — 20 in, 40 out — but we use the grinder to hit that 25–27 second window."
key_points: Grinder = time machine
Finer = slower shot
Coarser = faster shot
One change at a time
Purge after adjusting

student_questions.q: How much do I turn it?
student_questions.a: Start with the smallest increment available. It's surprising how sensitive it is.

student_questions.q: My grinder doesn't have numbers, how do I know where I am?
student_questions.a: Mark your current position with a sticker or tape until you know your grinder well.

checklist: Demonstrate a grind adjustment
Show before and after shot times
Have students make an adjustment themselves
Remind them to purge after adjusting

data.title: Distribution & Tamping
data.objective: Teach the importance of an even coffee bed before extraction.
data.content:
## Distribution & Tamping

### Why It Matters
Water is lazy. It always finds the easiest path. An uneven coffee bed creates channels — low-resistance paths where water rushes through, leaving other areas under-extracted.

Result: bitter and sour in the same shot.

### Distribution
1. Grind directly into portafilter
2. Tap the side gently once or twice to settle grounds
3. Use a distribution tool or finger to level the surface
4. Check for high/low points before tamping

### Tamping
1. Place portafilter on a flat surface
2. Apply level, even pressure — approximately 15–20kg
3. No rotation needed — just straight down, level
4. Check: the puck surface should be flat and even

### Common Mistakes
- Tamping at an angle
- Not distributing first
- Tapping the portafilter too hard (loosens the puck)
data.trainer_script: "Water is lazy — it will always find the easiest path through the coffee. If your coffee bed is uneven, the water rushes through the thin spots and barely touches the thick spots. You end up with one half sour and one half bitter in the same shot. Distribution before tamping is what prevents this."
key_points: Water follows the path of least resistance
Uneven bed = channelling = defective shot
Distribute before tamping
Tamp level with consistent pressure

student_questions.q: How hard should I tamp?
student_questions.a: About 15–20kg. If you're not sure, practice on scales.

student_questions.q: Do I need a special tool?
student_questions.a: A distribution tool helps but a finger can work at first.

checklist: Demonstrate distribution first
Show what an angled tamp looks like
Have students practice tamping on scales to feel correct pressure
Show a properly prepared puck

data.title: Milk Science
data.objective: Teach the science of milk texturing so trainers can explain it clearly.
data.content:
## Milk Science

Milk is made of fat, protein, and lactose (sugar). Understanding how these interact with heat and air helps trainers explain steaming clearly.

### The Two Phases of Steaming

Phase 1 — Stretching (Add Air)
Steam wand tip just below the surface. Air is introduced. Milk expands.
- Duration: First 5–8 seconds until milk reaches 37°C
- Sound: Gentle tearing or paper-tearing sound
- Goal: Increase milk volume by 30%

Phase 2 — Texturing (Integrate Air)
Steam wand tip deeper into milk. Create a whirlpool.
- Duration: Until 65–68°C (too hot to hold jug comfortably)
- Sound: Quiet hissing
- Goal: Integrate air into glossy microfoam

### What Perfect Milk Looks Like
Glossy, like wet paint. Pours slowly. No large bubbles visible.

### Common Mistakes
- Too much air = bubbly, won't pour cleanly
- Too little air = flat, won't hold pattern
- Too hot = scalded, tastes burnt, proteins destroyed
data.trainer_script: "Imagine wet paint on a brush. That's what perfect milk looks like — smooth, glossy, flows slowly. Big bubbles mean too much air was introduced. Flat milk means not enough. You want that in-between — like a thick glossy sauce."
key_points: Two phases: stretch then texture
Stretching = add air (near surface)
Texturing = integrate air (whirlpool)
Target temperature: 65–68°C
Goal: glossy wet paint texture

student_questions.q: Why does my milk look bubbly?
student_questions.a: Too much air in stretching phase. Keep the tip deeper.

student_questions.q: How do I know when it's hot enough?
student_questions.a: Can't hold the jug comfortably. Or use a thermometer — 65°C is ideal.

checklist: Demonstrate both phases separately
Let students feel the jug temperature
Show what over-aerated milk looks like vs ideal
Let students practice and correct one thing at a time

data.title: Latte Art Foundations
data.objective: Equip trainers to teach the fundamentals of latte art pouring.
data.content:
## Latte Art Foundations

Latte art requires three things to work: good crema, good milk texture, and pour control. Without the first two, pour control means nothing.

### The Pour Sequence
1. Check the canvas — Fresh espresso with intact crema
2. Start high — Hold jug 8–10cm above the cup
3. High pour sinks milk — Milk goes under the crema, building the base
4. Lower the jug — Bring tip to just above the surface
5. Move forward — Pour milk directly at the crema to draw the pattern
6. Cut through — Raise and slice forward at the end to create the point or split

### Basic Patterns
- Dot: Hold still at low pour. Round white circle.
- Heart: Dot, then slice forward through it.
- Tulip: Layer milk in stages, slice at end.
- Rosetta: Move the jug side to side while moving forward, then slice.

### Why Latte Art Fails
- Milk is wrong texture (too foamy or too flat)
- Crema has broken down (espresso too old)
- Pouring from too high (milk sinks, can't create pattern)
- Cup angle not used (no flow control)
data.trainer_script: "Before you try to pour a heart, check your canvas. If the crema is perfect and the milk is glossy — you're already 70% there. Start high to build the foundation, then come in low to draw the pattern. The milk does the work. You just direct it."
key_points: Canvas matters — good crema + good milk
Start high to sink milk below crema
Come low to draw the pattern
Cut through at the end
Teach dot and heart first

student_questions.q: Why does my milk just sink?
student_questions.a: Pouring too high, or milk not textured properly.

student_questions.q: How long does it take to learn?
student_questions.a: Most people can pour a recognisable heart in one session. A rosetta takes weeks of daily practice.

checklist: Demonstrate a heart pour slowly
Show where to start high and where to drop low
Have students practice the dot first
Correct one thing at a time per student

data.title: Student Troubleshooting
data.objective: Teach trainers to quickly diagnose and fix common student problems.
data.content:
## Student Troubleshooting Guide

### Espresso Problems

| Problem | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| Shot too fast (<22s) | Grind too coarse | Go finer |
| Shot too slow (>30s) | Grind too fine | Go coarser |
| Shot too little volume | Stopped too early | Wait for target weight |
| Channelling (blonde streak) | Uneven distribution | Re-distribute before tamping |
| Bitter taste | Over-extracted | Go coarser |
| Sour taste | Under-extracted | Go finer |

### Milk Problems

| Problem | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| Too bubbly | Too much air | Less time near surface |
| Too flat | Not enough air | Start near surface longer |
| Too hot | Steamed too long | Stop sooner / use thermometer |
| Separated | Let it sit too long | Use immediately after steaming |

### Latte Art Problems

| Problem | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| Pattern not appearing | Pouring too high | Bring jug closer |
| Pattern washed out | Milk too thick | Less air in stretch |
| Milk sinking entirely | Bad crema or wrong texture | Check espresso age and milk texture |

### Student Confidence Problems
- Nervous beginner → Praise effort, never the result. Lower expectations to build wins.
- Freezing up → Talk them through it step by step in real time.
- Getting frustrated → Redirect to one win. "Your tamp was perfect. Let's focus on just the pour."
data.trainer_script: "When a student is struggling, your first job is to identify ONE thing to fix. Not everything. Just one. If you give three corrections at once, they'll get overwhelmed and shut down. Pick the most impactful issue, correct that, let them repeat, then move on."
key_points: Diagnose before correcting
Fast shot = coarser; slow shot = finer
Bubbly milk = too much air; flat milk = too little
Pattern not appearing = too high or wrong milk
One correction at a time

student_questions.q: Why does my shot look different every time?
student_questions.a: Consistency takes time. Focus on the recipe — same dose, same grind — and it'll stabilise.

## Roastery Tour Knowledge

### The Tour Flow
1. Start at green beans — Show them raw coffee. Let them hold and smell.
2. Move to roasted beans — Contrast the smell and appearance.
3. Explain the Giesen roaster — Brief, visual, exciting.
4. Connect to what they'll taste today.

### Talking Points

Green beans:
"This is coffee before it becomes coffee. No smell, no flavour — just a seed. Everything that happens from here decides what ends up in your cup."

Roasted beans:
"Same bean, 12 minutes later at 200 degrees. That transformation creates hundreds of flavour compounds. This is where coffee actually becomes coffee."

Giesen roaster:
"This is a Giesen drum roaster — one of the most respected roasters in the industry. Every batch we run is profiled to match the specific bean's ideal development. It's precise, not guesswork."

### Soft Business Mention
"We train baristas here, but we also roast and supply coffee to cafés all over the city. If you ever open your own place or want to talk supply — we're happy to chat."

Do not push. Mention it once, naturally.
data.trainer_script: "The tour is not a lecture. It's a conversation with props. Let students touch things, smell things, ask questions. The Giesen is a visual anchor — even if they don't understand how it works, it signals professionalism. Make them feel like they're behind the scenes somewhere special."

data.title: How to Control the Room
data.objective: Teach trainers to lead the energy and control the pace of a class.
data.content:
## How to Control the Room

### From the First Minute
The first 60 seconds sets the tone for the whole class. Walk in with energy. Introduce yourself like you mean it. Learn every student's name immediately.

### The Three Room Controls
1. Physical control — Where you stand, how you move, how you use the equipment space
2. Pace control — Moving fast when energy drops, slowing down for complex moments
3. Attention control — Direct questions, demos, and personal feedback keep students engaged

### Name Power
Using a student's name when giving feedback is one of the most powerful engagement tools. "Marcus, that tamp was perfect" lands differently than "Good tamp everyone."
data.trainer_script: "The moment you walk in, students decide whether they trust you. Not because of what you say — because of how you carry yourself. Stand straight, look confident, smile genuinely, and speak like you've done this a thousand times. Even if it's your third class ever."
key_points: First 60 seconds sets the tone
Learn names before class if possible
Move around the space — don't stand in one spot
Use names when giving feedback
checklist: Know names before class
Plan your opening line
Move between all students during practice

data.title: Show, Explain, Do, Correct
data.objective: Master the core teaching sequence for all practical skills.
data.content:
## Show, Explain, Do, Correct

This is the teaching sequence for every practical skill in a Bean Culture course.

### The Sequence
1. Show — Trainer demonstrates the skill in full, at full speed
2. Explain — Trainer demonstrates again, slowly, narrating each step
3. Do — Student attempts the skill
4. Correct — Trainer identifies ONE issue and addresses it specifically
5. Repeat — Student does it again incorporating the correction

### Why One Correction Only
The human brain can only process one new physical instruction at a time. If you correct the hand position AND the pour angle AND the milk texture simultaneously, the student will freeze.

Pick the most impactful correction. Apply it. Watch improvement. Move to the next issue next time.
data.trainer_script: "Watch me first. Then I'll show you again and explain what I'm doing. Then it's your turn. After your first attempt, I'm going to give you one thing to focus on — just one. We'll work through corrections one at a time."
key_points: Show full speed, then slow with narration
Student attempts after seeing twice
One correction only per attempt
Let them repeat before adding more feedback
checklist: Demonstrate at full speed first
Demonstrate slowly with narration
Observe student attempt fully before correcting
Identify single most impactful correction

data.title: Micro-Corrections
data.objective: Learn to give targeted, specific corrections that improve quickly.
data.content:
## Micro-Corrections

Never overload students. The art of teaching is choosing the right correction at the right moment.

### What to Correct (In Priority Order)
1. Safety issues — always first
2. Recipe accuracy (dose, yield, time)
3. Distribution and tamping technique
4. Pour height
5. Milk texture
6. Cup angle
7. Pattern detail

### How to Correct
- Never say: "That's wrong" / "No, not like that"
- Always say: "Try this instead" / "Small adjustment here" / "Let's shift this slightly"

Physical corrections: Always ask permission first. "Can I show you the hand position?"
data.trainer_script: "I'm going to stop you — not because you're doing badly, but because I can see exactly what will make your next attempt 50% better. Just this one thing."
key_points: Safety first, always
Recipe accuracy second
One correction, framed positively
Ask permission before physical correction
checklist: Identify one issue per attempt
Frame corrections positively
Ask permission before touching student's technique

## Conversation Padding

Silence during practice can feel tense. These phrases fill natural gaps and maintain positive energy.

### Encouragement Lines
- "That's better than most first attempts."
- "You're closer than you think."
- "Small change, big difference."
- "This is where it usually clicks."
- "Every barista struggles with this at first."
- "Speed comes after consistency."

### Transition Lines

### Closing Lines

- "You came in today not knowing how to pull an espresso. You're leaving as someone who can."

Closing lines should acknowledge growth

data.title: Handling Different Student Types
data.objective: Teach trainers to adapt to the full range of student personalities.
data.content:
## Handling Different Student Types

### Nervous Beginner
Signs: hesitation, asking lots of questions, apologising
Approach: Lower the bar. Give them an easy win immediately. "Just pour this shot over ice — no latte art today, just get comfortable with the machine."

### Overconfident Student
Signs: rushing, not listening, saying "I know"
Approach: Respect their confidence, redirect with specifics. "You clearly have instinct — let's focus it on the recipe and see how that changes things."

### Quiet Student
Signs: not asking questions, seems disengaged
Approach: Direct but gentle questions. "What did that taste like to you?" Don't call them out publicly.

### Home Hobbyist
Goal: Better home coffee, not employment
Approach: More relaxed, connect everything to their home setup. "On your machine at home, you'd do this..."

### Future Café Worker
Goal: Employment confidence
Approach: Focus on speed, workflow, and professional standards. "In a café, this is how you'd communicate an order."

### Café Owner
Goal: Better understanding for quality control
Approach: Treat as a peer. Explain at a higher level. Discuss wholesale and ongoing supply.
data.trainer_script: "You won't always get a room of eager learners. You'll get people who are scared, people who think they already know everything, people who are quiet, people who won't stop talking. Your job is to read the room and adapt — every class, every student."
key_points: Read each student's motivation within the first 15 minutes
Adapt your approach — not your content
Nervous = give early wins
Overconfident = redirect with precision
Quiet = gentle direct questions
checklist: Identify each student's type by 0:20
Adjust energy and communication style per student
Ensure every student gets individual attention

data.title: Gamification
data.objective: Use challenges and competition to increase engagement and enjoyment.
data.content:
## Gamification

Gamification makes the class more memorable and energises the practice phase.

### Challenges to Use
- Best Pour Challenge — Who pours the best-looking pattern at the end?
- Fastest Dial-In — Who can hit the recipe first?
- Palate Challenge — Guess under/over/balanced blind tasting
- Before/After Photo — Document their worst and best pour
- Best Improvement Award — Recognise biggest growth, not best result

### When to Use Gamification
- Energy drops mid-class
- Students are struggling and need a reset
- Near the end as a fun finale
- When you have a competitive group

### Rules
- Always celebrate improvement, not just results
- Never embarrass struggling students
- Make the "winner" about effort, not talent
data.trainer_script: "Right — we're going to have a little challenge. Best pour wins... absolutely nothing except the respect of the room. Go."
key_points: Use challenges when energy drops
Best improvement > best result
Keep it light and fun
Before/after photos make progress visible
checklist: Plan one gamification moment per class
Have a prize or recognition ready
Photo the best/worst pour comparison

data.title: Handling Questions You Don't Know
data.objective: Teach trainers to handle unknown questions with confidence and honesty.
data.content:
## Handling Questions You Don't Know

New trainers often panic when asked something they don't know. Here is the correct approach:

### The Right Response
"That's a great question. I want to give you the correct answer rather than guessing. Let me check that properly and get back to you."

Then actually follow up — by message, email, or the next class.

### Why This Works
- Students respect honesty far more than confident guessing
- A wrong answer delivered with confidence is still wrong — and destroys trust
- Following up shows you care

### Build Your Knowledge Base
As you train more classes, you'll build a library of answers. Keep notes on questions you get. Review the Train the Trainer lessons after each class to fill your gaps.

### What Never to Do
- Guess and state it as fact
- Say "I don't know" without committing to finding out
- Change the subject to avoid the question
data.trainer_script: "That's a great question. I want to give you the correct answer, so I'll check that properly rather than guessing. I'll get back to you on that."
key_points: Honesty beats confident guessing
Commit to following up — and do it
Keep notes on questions you can't answer
Review knowledge base after each class
checklist: Keep a notepad for unknown questions
Review answers before next class
Follow up with students who asked

data.objective: Establish the standards that make every Bean Culture class feel exceptional.
data.content:
## Premium Experience Rules

Every Bean Culture class must feel premium, professional, and personal. This is not optional — it's the brand.

### Non-Negotiables
1. Clean workspace — Set up before students arrive. Nothing looks amateur like scrambling at the start.
2. Music playing — Background music during practice changes the energy of the room.
3. Friendly tone — Not formal, not casual. Warm and professional.
4. Personal feedback — Every student gets individual feedback on something they did well.
5. Photo moment — Capture their best pour or a moment with their espresso.
6. Certificate moment — Present the certificate. Don't just hand it over. Make it feel earned.
7. Review request — Ask genuinely. "If you enjoyed today, a Google review helps us a lot."

### The Certificate Moment
"Before you leave, I want to present this to you. You came in today with zero experience and you're leaving able to make a real espresso, texture milk, and attempt latte art. That's not small. That's worth recognising."
data.trainer_script: "The certificate moment is the emotional peak of the class. Don't rush it. Say their name. Say what they achieved. Hand it over with both hands if you can. Students remember this moment."
key_points: Set up before students arrive
Music during practice
Every student gets individual praise
Photo of best pour
Certificate presented — not just handed over
Review request is natural, not pushy

Trainers are not salespeople. But they are brand ambassadors.

- Bean Culture coffee beans (retail)

- Advanced training courses
- Booking another course

The best marketing is a great class

data.title: Student Confidence Building
data.objective: Learn the mindset techniques that build lasting student confidence.
data.content:
## Student Confidence Building

Most students arrive nervous. Many have never used a commercial espresso machine. Your job is to make the unfamiliar feel achievable.

### The Confidence Cycle
1. Create a small win early
2. Name it explicitly: "You just pulled a real espresso. That's real."
3. Build on that win with the next step
4. Repeat

### Language Matters
- Don't say: "Wrong" / "Bad" / "No" / "That's not right"
- Do say: "Try this adjustment" / "Let's shift this slightly" / "Almost — one small thing"

### The Before/After Reveal
At the end of class, remind students what they couldn't do at the start. "Two hours ago, you didn't know what 20g in 40g out meant. Now you can pull a shot on a commercial machine and pour milk. That's real progress."

### Praise Effort, Not Talent
"You worked hard on that" lands better than "You're a natural." Effort is something they can control and repeat.
data.trainer_script: "Before you leave today, I want you to hear this: what you've done in the last few hours would have taken most people weeks of daily practice at home to achieve. You've done it in one session. That's a real thing."
key_points: Create a small win in the first 20 minutes
Name wins explicitly and specifically
Use positive language only for corrections
Before/after reveal at end of class
Praise effort, not talent
checklist: Plan an easy early win for nervous students
Prepare a closing statement acknowledging each student's growth
End on a high — never let class trail off

data.question: What is coffee technically?
data.explanation: Coffee is technically the seed found inside the coffee cherry fruit.

data.question: What is Bean Culture's espresso recipe?
data.explanation: The Bean Culture recipe is 20g in, 40g out, 25–27 seconds.

data.question: If a shot runs too fast, what should the trainer adjust?
data.explanation: A fast shot means insufficient resistance. Grinding finer creates more surface area and slows the water down.

data.question: If coffee tastes bitter and harsh, it is most likely:
data.explanation: Bitter and harsh flavours are characteristic of over-extraction — too many bitter compounds have been drawn out.

data.question: What should ideal steamed milk texture look like?
data.explanation: Perfect microfoam should look glossy and smooth, like wet paint — no visible bubbles.

data.question: What should a trainer correct first if latte art is not appearing?
data.explanation: Milk texture and pour height are the two most impactful factors for latte art. Without correct milk, no pour technique will work.

data.question: What is the correct teaching order?
data.explanation: Show (full speed), Explain (narrated), Do (student attempt), Correct (one thing) is the correct sequence.

data.question: What should trainers avoid saying to students?
data.explanation: Negative language like 'wrong' or 'bad' damages student confidence. Always frame corrections positively.

data.question: Which processing method produces the cleanest, brightest cup with the most transparent terroir?
data.explanation: Washed (wet) processing removes all fruit before drying, producing a clean, bright cup that lets the bean's terroir shine.

data.question: Which processing method is most likely to produce fruity, wine-like, heavy-bodied coffee?
data.explanation: Natural processing dries the whole cherry, imparting fruity and wine-like characteristics to the bean.

data.question: In what order do compounds extract during espresso pulling?
data.explanation: Acids extract first (brightness), then sugars (sweetness and body), then bitter compounds last.

data.question: Under-extracted espresso typically tastes:
data.explanation: Under-extraction pulls mainly acids before the sugars develop, resulting in sour, thin, and hollow flavour.

data.question: Arabica coffee typically grows at:
data.explanation: Arabica requires high altitude (600–2000m), cooler temperatures, and specific rainfall to develop its complex flavours.

data.question: Compared to Robusta, Arabica generally has:
options: Less caffeine and more complex flavour
The same caffeine and richer body
data.explanation: Arabica has about half the caffeine of Robusta and a far more complex, nuanced flavour profile.

data.question: Light roast coffee typically has:
options: Less caffeine and less origin character
More caffeine and more origin character
More roast character and less acidity
data.explanation: Light roasting preserves more of the bean's natural origin character and slightly more caffeine.

data.question: At what temperature does second crack typically occur during roasting?
data.explanation: Second crack occurs at approximately 218°C+, marking the transition into dark roast territory.

data.question: At what temperature should milk steaming stop?
data.explanation: 65–68°C is optimal. Above 70°C, milk proteins denature and sweetness is destroyed.

data.question: During the stretching phase of steaming, where should the steam wand tip be positioned?
options: Deep in the milk, pointing down
At the centre of the jug
data.explanation: The tip should be just below the surface during stretching to introduce air gently.

data.question: Large bubbles in steamed milk indicate:
data.explanation: Large visible bubbles result from introducing too much air too quickly during the stretching phase.

data.question: After adjusting the grinder setting, what must a barista do before pulling the next shot?
data.explanation: Purging clears the grinder channel of old grounds from the previous setting, ensuring a consistent dose.

data.question: A shot that stops at 36–37g on the scale will typically yield approximately:
data.explanation: Drip-through after stopping adds 3–4g, so stopping at 36–37g lands the final yield at approximately 40g.

data.question: How many corrections should a trainer give per student attempt?
data.explanation: One correction per attempt. The brain can only process one new physical instruction at a time.

Create an early easy win to build confidence
Pair them with the most confident student
data.explanation: An early easy win — something they can succeed at immediately — builds the confidence needed for harder skills.

Origin character increases with roast level
Dark roast beans are always from low-altitude farms

data.question: Why might milk pour straight down through the crema without forming a pattern?

data.explanation: Undertextured milk (too thin or flat) sinks straight through the crema without creating enough contrast to form a pattern.
